papers.title: Quantifying the relationship between exposure to natural disasters and early-childhood immunization in low- and middle-income countries.
papers.abstract: Limited research has explored the relationship between exposure to natural hazards and antenatal and early childhood vaccination indicators. We leveraged individual-level data from Young Lives: An International Study of Childhood Poverty surveys conducted in 2002 to estimate the association of household exposure to natural disaster in Ethiopia, India (in the states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana), Peru, and Vietnam on antenatal and early childhood vaccinations among mother/child pairs. We ran mixed-effects logistic regression models with interaction between exposure to natural disaster and vaccine type (≥ 2 doses of antenatal tetanus during antenatal visits, postnatal BCG [Bacillus Calmette-Guérin], postnatal measles), controlled for wealth index and child age as fixed effects, and included nested random effects with country, sentinel site, and individual ID. We found that the association between exposure to natural disaster and vaccination varied by vaccine type. Exposure to natural disaster was associated with an increased probability of receiving ≥ 2 doses of antenatal tetanus vaccine during antenatal visits of 5.75 percentage points (estimate: 0.0575; 95% CI: 0.0186, 0.0964), and a decreased probability of receiving postnatal BCG vaccine against tuberculosis of 3.11 percentage points (estimate: -0.0311; 95% CI: -0.0576, -0.00455). We did not find a significant association for postnatal measles vaccination (estimate: 0.00647; 95% CI: -0.03, 0.0429). This study finds that exposure to natural disasters is associated with antenatal and early childhood vaccination, underscoring the importance of increasing immunization efforts for specific vaccines in areas recently affected by natural disasters. However, further studies are needed to verify results and establish causation.

papers.source_body_en: Limited research has explored the relationship between exposure to natural hazards and antenatal and early childhood vaccination indicators. We leveraged individual-level data from Young Lives: An International Study of Childhood Poverty surveys conducted in 2002 to estimate the association of household exposure to natural disaster in Ethiopia, India (in the states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana), Peru, and Vietnam on antenatal and early childhood vaccinations among mother/child pairs. We ran mixed-effects logistic regression models with interaction between exposure to natural disaster and vaccine type (≥ 2 doses of antenatal tetanus during antenatal visits, postnatal BCG [Bacillus Calmette-Guérin], postnatal measles), controlled for wealth index and child age as fixed effects, and included nested random effects with country, sentinel site, and individual ID. We found that the association between exposure to natural disaster and vaccination varied by vaccine type. Exposure to natural disaster was associated with an increased probability of receiving ≥ 2 doses of antenatal tetanus vaccine during antenatal visits of 5.75 percentage points (estimate: 0.0575; 95% CI: 0.0186, 0.0964), and a decreased probability of receiving postnatal BCG vaccine against tuberculosis of 3.11 percentage points (estimate: -0.0311; 95% CI: -0.0576, -0.00455). We did not find a significant association for postnatal measles vaccination (estimate: 0.00647; 95% CI: -0.03, 0.0429). This study finds that exposure to natural disasters is associated with antenatal and early childhood vaccination, underscoring the importance of increasing immunization efforts for specific vaccines in areas recently affected by natural disasters. However, further studies are needed to verify results and establish causation.

papers.title: GAPS in Protection Against Vaccine-Preventable Infections in Patients Post-Haematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant for Primary Immunodeficiency Syndromes.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Patients with primary immunodeficiency (PID) syndromes are susceptible to vaccine-preventable infections post-haematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT). Timely re-immunisation following immune reconstitution is critical. METHOD: HSCTs conducted 2018-2025 at Starship Children's Hospital (New Zealand) to treat children (age ≤18 years) were identified through the institutional database. Local and national electronic medical records, clinical and laboratory data, and vaccination records (Aotearoa Immunisation Register) were reviewed. Post-HSCT re-immunisation eligibility criteria and audit standards were based on National Child Cancer Network NZ guidelines. RESULTS: Of 197 unique patients who received 236 HSCTs, 28 patients had PID as the reason for HSCT. Patients were excluded if they were not currently cleared for re-immunisation for clinical reasons (n = 2) or died within 6 months of HSCT (n = 4). Twenty-two patients who were eligible for re-immunisation were included for this preliminary report. One of 22 (4.5%) had not commenced re-immunisation. Median time between the date of clearance for re-immunisation and administration of the first non-live vaccine was 64 days (interquartile range [IQR] 9-126 days). Deviation from standard vaccination sequence occurred in 33% of patients (7/21). At any one visit, 85% (18/21) were not given all eligible vaccines. 9% (2/22) were fully up-to-date with re-immunisations at the time of audit. Twenty patients were eligible for live vaccines. 65% (13/20) were given at least one dose of a measles-containing vaccine (MCV). Median time between last blood product administration and first dose of MCV was 669 days (IQR 476-766 days). 50% (10/20) received 2 doses of MCV. 40% (4/10) had post-MCV measles serology checked; one individual remained seronegative despite 2 doses of MCV. CONCLUSION: Completion of re-immunisation schedules post-HSCT is suboptimal, leaving gaps in protection against vaccine-preventable infections. There is considerable delay between clearance for re-immunisation and commencement. Uptake of MCV and the practice of confirming seroconversion is highly variable.

analysis.summary_en: This review focuses on gaps in protection against measles virus and related vaccine-preventable infections in patients post-haematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) for primary immunodeficiency (PID) syndromes. The study analyzed HSCTs conducted at Starship Children's Hospital in New Zealand between 2018 and 2025, focusing on children aged ≤18 years. The review highlights that re-immunisation schedules post-HSCT are suboptimal, with delays in vaccine commencement and variability in measles-containing vaccine (MCV) uptake. Only 9% of patients were fully up-to-date with re-immunisations, and 40% had post-MCV measles serology checked, with one individual remaining seronegative despite two doses. These findings underscore the need for improved adherence to vaccination protocols and further research on vaccine effectiveness in this vulnerable population.

papers.title_zh: 原发性免疫缺陷综合征患者造血干细胞移植后预防 疫苗 可预防感染的差距。
papers.source_body_en: INTRODUCTION: Patients with primary immunodeficiency (PID) syndromes are susceptible to vaccine-preventable infections post-haematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT). Timely re-immunisation following immune reconstitution is critical. METHOD: HSCTs conducted 2018-2025 at Starship Children's Hospital (New Zealand) to treat children (age ≤18 years) were identified through the institutional database. Local and national electronic medical records, clinical and laboratory data, and vaccination records (Aotearoa Immunisation Register) were reviewed. Post-HSCT re-immunisation eligibility criteria and audit standards were based on National Child Cancer Network NZ guidelines. RESULTS: Of 197 unique patients who received 236 HSCTs, 28 patients had PID as the reason for HSCT. Patients were excluded if they were not currently cleared for re-immunisation for clinical reasons (n = 2) or died within 6 months of HSCT (n = 4). Twenty-two patients who were eligible for re-immunisation were included for this preliminary report. One of 22 (4.5%) had not commenced re-immunisation. Median time between the date of clearance for re-immunisation and administration of the first non-live vaccine was 64 days (interquartile range [IQR] 9-126 days). Deviation from standard vaccination sequence occurred in 33% of patients (7/21). At any one visit, 85% (18/21) were not given all eligible vaccines. 9% (2/22) were fully up-to-date with re-immunisations at the time of audit. Twenty patients were eligible for live vaccines. 65% (13/20) were given at least one dose of a measles-containing vaccine (MCV). Median time between last blood product administration and first dose of MCV was 669 days (IQR 476-766 days). 50% (10/20) received 2 doses of MCV. 40% (4/10) had post-MCV measles serology checked; one individual remained seronegative despite 2 doses of MCV. CONCLUSION: Completion of re-immunisation schedules post-HSCT is suboptimal, leaving gaps in protection against vaccine-preventable infections. There is considerable delay between clearance for re-immunisation and commencement. Uptake of MCV and the practice of confirming seroconversion is highly variable.

papers.title: Prevalence of diarrhea and its determinants among children under five years of age in rural Kebeles of East Gurage Zone, central Ethiopia: A cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Diarrheal disease remains a major cause of death among children under five, particularly in resource-limited settings. Despite the availability of effective water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions, the burden of diarrhea remains high in Ethiopia. This study aims to assess the prevalence of diarrhea and its associated factors among under-five children in East Gurage Zone, central Ethiopia. METHODOLOGY: This baseline survey was part of a four-arm cluster randomized trial (cRCT). Using the Hayes and Bennett formula, we set the sample size at 840 participants (210 per arm) with 95% confidence and 80% power. Data were cleaned in Epi Data 3.1 and analyzed in SPSS 25. Reliability testing showed weak internal consistency, with Cronbach's alpha of 0.36 for knowledge, 0.46 for practice, and 0.40 for wealth, reflecting few items and distinct domains. Childhood diarrhea associated factors were examined using bivariate and multivariate Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) models, accounting for clustering, with significance set at p < 0.05 and 95% CI. RESULTS: Diarrhea prevalence was high in the study area (25.7%) (95% CI: 22.8-28.7). Maternal age 24-34 (AOR = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.27-0.53), hand washing at critical times (AOR = 0.20, 95% CI: 0.07-0.58), both soap and water use (AOR = 0.09, 95% CI: 0.03-0.33), using tightly covered (AOR = 0.17, 95% CI: 0.03-0.91) and clean water containers (AOR = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.26-0.84), measles vaccination (AOR = 0.07, 95% CI: 0.04-0.13), fetching water <30 minutes round-trip (AOR = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.12-0.57), and latrine availability (AOR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.19-0.43) were significantly associated with lower odds of under-five diarrhea. CONCLUSION: Diarrhea affected one in four children (25.7%; 95% CI: 22.8-28.7), indicating a substantial burden in the study area, particularly in rural communities. Strengthening WASH interventions and fostering coordinated efforts among government, local authorities, and development partners is essential to reduce this burden. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07158632.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study aimed to assess the prevalence of diarrhea and its associated factors among under-five children in rural Kebeles of East Gurage Zone, central Ethiopia. The study was part of a four-arm cluster randomized trial with a sample size of 840 participants. Data were analyzed using SPSS 25, and reliability testing showed weak internal consistency for knowledge, practice, and wealth domains. Diarrhea prevalence was found to be high at 25.7% (95% CI: 22.8-28.7). Factors significantly associated with lower odds of under-five diarrhea included maternal age 24-34, hand washing at critical times, both soap and water use, using tightly covered and clean water containers, measles vaccination, fetching water <30 minutes round-trip, and latrine availability. The authors concluded that strengthening WASH interventions and fostering coordinated efforts among government, local authorities, and development partners is essential to reduce the burden of diarrhea. The study's findings are limited by the weak internal consistency of the reliability testing, and the evidence is moderate in strength.

papers.title: Incidence of Infectious Diseases in Bulgaria over a 50-Year Period (1974–2023)
papers.abstract: Objective: To investigate the long-term trends and dynamics of acute infectious diseases morbidity in Bulgaria across half of century of significant socio-economic transitions, healthcare reforms, and geopolitical integrations. Methods: retrospective epidemiological study was conducted covering a 50-year period (1974–2023). Aggregated data from 10 consecutive five-year cohorts were extracted from official statutory reporting networks managed by the National Statistical Institute (NSI), the National Center for Public Health and Analyses (NCPHA), and the National Center for Infectious and Parasitic Diseases (NCIPD). Results: Drastic shifts in infectious disease dynamics correlate directly with national immunization strategies, economic transitions, and the entry into force of healthcare reforms. Mass immunoprophylaxis achieved successful elimination patterns or historic minimums for core respiratory and neuro-invasive pathogens, including diphtheria and rubella. However, recent 2020-2023 metrics reveal sub-optimal measles-mumpsrubella (MMR) and pertussis coverage, sparking a notable upward trend in pertussis morbidity and infant mortality. Pathogens lacking mass vaccination frameworks, such as varicella and scarlet fever, exhibited sharp post-pandemic resurgences following the relaxation of containment measures. Climate-driven shifts are expanding vector-borne footprints, such as West Nile fever. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic introduced substantial diagnostic reporting artefacts and a heavy excess mortality burden. Conclusions: Long-term surveillance data confirms a persistent overall decline in vaccine-preventable diseases alongside expanding relative shares of intestinal, emerging vector-borne, and non-vaccine-preventable respiratory infections. Tracking these dynamics provides a vital public health baseline for mitigating vaccine hesitancy and changing ecological disease boundaries.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 进行了一项涵盖 50 年(1974 年至 2023 年)的回顾性流行病学研究。

elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 长期 监测 数据证实,疫苗 可预防疾病的总体持续下降,同时肠道、新出现的 媒介 传播的疾病和非 疫苗 可预防的呼吸道感染的相对比例不断扩大。跟踪这些动态为减轻 疫苗 犹豫和改变生态疾病边界提供了重要的公共卫生基线。

papers.title: Viral Pathogens as Global Health Threats: Review of Transmissibility, Lethality, and Pandemic Potential
papers.abstract: Viral pathogens vary substantially in their transmissibility, lethality, and potential to cause widespread epidemics or pandemics. Measles, for example, is exceptionally contagious but has relatively low case fatality in populations with access to modern medical care. Conversely, rabies, Nipah virus, Ebola virus, and Marburg virus can cause severe disease with high case fatality rates but generally exhibit limited sustained human-to-human transmission. The greatest global threats, therefore, are not necessarily the most contagious or lethal viruses, but those that combine efficient transmission, substantial clinical severity, zoonotic reservoirs, evolutionary adaptability, and limited preventive or therapeutic options. The COVID-19 pandemic illustrated this convergence of risk factors, demonstrating how efficient transmission, including presymptomatic and asymptomatic spread, coupled with clinically significant disease can produce devastating global consequences. Influenza A viruses remain a major pandemic concern because of their extensive animal reservoirs, capacity for antigenic evolution, and established history of human pandemics. Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) is particularly concerning given the high case fatality observed among confirmed human cases, although sustained human-to-human transmission has not been established. In contrast, henipaviruses and filoviruses pose substantial clinical threats because of their high lethality, despite comparatively limited transmissibility. This review critically examines major viral threats through three interconnected determinants of global health risk: transmissibility, infection fatality risk, and the biological and epidemiological factors governing their epidemic and pandemic potential.

Measles, for example, is exceptionally contagious but has relatively low case fatality in populations with access to modern medical care. Conversely, rabies, Nipah virus, Ebola virus, and Marburg virus can cause severe disease with high case fatality rates but generally exhibit limited sustained human-to-human transmission. The greatest global threats, therefore, are not necessarily the most contagious or lethal viruses, but those that combine efficient transmission, substantial clinical severity, zoonotic reservoirs, evolutionary adaptability, and limited preventive or therapeutic options. The COVID-19 pandemic illustrated this convergence of risk factors, demonstrating how efficient transmission, including presymptomatic and asymptomatic spread, coupled with clinically significant disease can produce devastating global consequences. Influenza A viruses remain a major pandemic concern because of their extensive animal reservoirs, capacity for antigenic evolution, and established history of human pandemics. Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) is particularly concerning given the high case fatality observed among confirmed human cases, although sustained human-to-human transmission has not been established. In contrast, henipaviruses and filoviruses pose substantial clinical threats because of their high lethality, despite comparatively limited transmissibility. This review critically examines major viral threats through three interconnected determinants of global health risk: transmissibility, infection fatality risk, and the biological and epidemiological factors governing their epidemic and pandemic potential.

papers.abstract_zh: 病毒病原体的传播性、致死性以及引起广泛流行病或大流行的可能性差异很大。例如,麻疹 具有极高的传染性,但在能够获得现代医疗护理的人群中病死率相对较低。相反,狂犬病、尼帕病毒、埃博拉病毒和马尔堡病毒可引起严重疾病,病死率高,但通常表现出有限的持续人际传播 传播。因此,最大的全球威胁不一定是最具传染性或致命性的病毒,而是那些结合了有效的 传播、临床严重性、人畜共患 储存宿主、进化适应性和有限的预防或治疗选择的病毒。COVID-19大流行说明了风险因素的这种融合,证明了传播的有效性,包括症状前和无症状传播,再加上临床上重大疾病,可以产生毁灭性的全球后果。甲型流感病毒由于其广泛的动物 储存宿主、抗原 进化 的能力以及人类大流行的历史,仍然是一个主要的大流行问题。尽管尚未确定持续的人传人 传播,但鉴于在已确诊的人类病例中观察到高病死率,高致病性甲型禽流感 (H5N1) 尤其令人担忧。相比之下,亨尼帕病毒和丝状病毒尽管传播能力相对有限,但由于其高致死率而构成重大临床威胁。本综述通过全球健康风险的三个相互关联的决定因素批判性地审查了主要的病毒威胁:传播性、感染死亡风险以及控制其流行和大流行潜力的生物和流行病学因素。

papers.title: An Ancient p53–miR-128 Axis Restricts Mucosal and Placental Viral Entry by Suppressing Nectin-4
papers.abstract: Host cell-surface receptors dictate viral tropism, tissue entry, and cross-barrier transmission. Although Nectin-4 (encoded by PVRL4) has recently been established as the essential epithelial receptor for major respiratory and teratogenic pathogens—including Measles virus and Rubella virus—the endogenous host mechanisms governing its expression remain poorly defined. Because physical wet-lab experimentation is absent in this study, we utilize advanced computational systems-biology modeling, network integration, and predictive multi-omics simulations. Here, we uncover an evolutionarily conserved host restriction pathway wherein the ancient antiviral guardian p53 coordinates with the longevity factor FOXO3a to deploy microRNA-128 (miR-128), which post-transcriptionally silences PVRL4. Systematic in silico evaluation of public expression repositories (GEO/Harmonizome) reveals a robust inverse correlation between p53 pathway activation states and PVRL4 surface density across polarized airway epithelia. By modeling the repression of surface Nectin-4 density, this predictive axis blocks the receptor-mediated membrane fusion required by Nectin-4-tropic viruses. These computational findings position the p53–FOXO3a–miR-128–Nectin-4 axis as a vital mucosal defense mechanism, demonstrating how ancient host restriction networks target specialized viral entry portals.

papers.source_body_en: Host cell-surface receptors dictate viral tropism, tissue entry, and cross-barrier transmission. Although Nectin-4 (encoded by PVRL4) has recently been established as the essential epithelial receptor for major respiratory and teratogenic pathogens—including Measles virus and Rubella virus—the endogenous host mechanisms governing its expression remain poorly defined. Because physical wet-lab experimentation is absent in this study, we utilize advanced computational systems-biology modeling, network integration, and predictive multi-omics simulations. Here, we uncover an evolutionarily conserved host restriction pathway wherein the ancient antiviral guardian p53 coordinates with the longevity factor FOXO3a to deploy microRNA-128 (miR-128), which post-transcriptionally silences PVRL4. Systematic in silico evaluation of public expression repositories (GEO/Harmonizome) reveals a robust inverse correlation between p53 pathway activation states and PVRL4 surface density across polarized airway epithelia. By modeling the repression of surface Nectin-4 density, this predictive axis blocks the receptor-mediated membrane fusion required by Nectin-4-tropic viruses. These computational findings position the p53–FOXO3a–miR-128–Nectin-4 axis as a vital mucosal defense mechanism, demonstrating how ancient host restriction networks target specialized viral entry portals.

papers.full_text: Addressing vaccine hesitancy in pulmonary disease training Until recently, vaccines have been largely regarded as a major triumph of medicine. According to estimates from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), between 1994 and 2023 childhood vaccines prevented roughly 508 million lifetime illnesses, 32 million hospitalizations, and 1,129,000 deaths, and netted $540 billion savings in direct costs and $2.7 trillion in societal costs. Yet vaccine hesitancy, defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as the delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite availability of vaccination services, is a mounting global phenomenon. It is therefore vital for healthcare providers, and specifically pulmonary disease specialists, to be deliberately trained not just in immunization science and epidemiology, but in the sources of vaccine hesitancy and evidence-based methods to overcome it. Vaccine hesitancy and opposition to vaccine implementation are as old as vaccines themselves, though the sources of concern have shifted over time. For example, early attempts to control smallpox with “inoculation” were met with religious objections, and in later decades, even the medical establishment was dubious of vaccine efficacy due to limited understanding of the role microbes play in disease and the immune system. Today, vaccine hesitancy stems mostly from misinformation and disinformation amplified by social media, which finds fertile soil in an increasingly polarized political climate. This fuels mistrust of healthcare providers and organizations, as noted by a 31.4% reduction of public trust in physicians and hospitals from April 2020 to January 2024, with lower levels of trust associated with refusal of COVID-19 vaccination. This can have far-reaching impacts as demonstrated by the 2025 recrudescence of measles in the United States and Canada attributed to suboptimal vaccination rates. Traditionally, contending with vaccine hesitancy relied on public trust in medical experts. A 1914 address by Sir William Osler to British troops at the outset of World War I serves as a historical example of countering vaccine hesitancy. In his speech “Bacilli and Bullets,” Osler took a pragmatic approach by appealing to reason with epidemiologic and scientific facts, stating, “What I wish to urge is a true knowledge of your foes, not simply of the bullets, but of the much more important enemy—the bacilli.” Osler was alluding to the fact that in the Second Boer War (1899-1902), typhoid was responsible for 64% of the 22,000 British lives lost despite the availability of an effective vaccine developed by Sir Almroth Wright. However, in this present era of undermined trust in expertise and erosion of confidence in established medicine, this approach has not been successful. How, then, are healthcare educators to address vaccine hesitancy? First and foremost, understanding reasons for vaccine hesitancy is paramount. A WHO framework categorizes determinants of vaccine hesitancy into contextual, individual, and group influences, and vaccine-related concerns (Table 1). Specific vaccine myths include the superiority of “natural” immunity, the concept of immune system overload/weakening, vaccine inefficacy, false or overestimated risk of adverse side effects (ie, autistic spectrum disorder), and customizing vaccine schedules to accommodate “too many” vaccines. The World Health Organization’s determinants of vaccine hesitancy. Determinants Examples Contextual influences: Influences arising due to historic, sociocultural, environmental, health system/institutional, economic or political factors Communication and media environmentInfluential leaders, gatekeepers, and anti- or pro-vaccination lobbiesHistorical influencesReligion/culture/gender/socioeconomicPolitics/policiesGeographic barriersPharmaceutical industry Individual and group influences: Influences arising from personal perception of the vaccine or influences of the social/peer environment Experience with past vaccinationBeliefs and attitudes about health and preventionKnowledge/awarenessHealth system and providers—trust and personal experienceRisk/benefit (perceived, heuristic)Immunization as a social norm vs not needed/harmful Vaccination-specific issues: Directly related to vaccine or vaccination Risk/benefit (perceived, heuristic)Immunization as a social norm vs not needed/harmfulRisk/benefit (scientific evidence)Introduction of a new vaccine or new formulationMode of administrationDesign of vaccination program/mode of deliveryReliability and/or source of vaccine supplyVaccination scheduleCostsRole of healthcare professionals Understandably, the pediatric field is leading the effort to reverse the vaccine hesitancy course as vaccines have been recommended for 18 vaccine-preventable diseases between the newborn period and adolescence. Initially, pediatric resident immunization education lacked consistency, as noted in a 2014 survey completed by 92 Association of Pediatric Program Directors members that revealed 59% of the programs lacked formal training on vaccine safety to address parental concerns. The American Academy of Pediatrics is therefore working to reduce vaccine hesitancy by strengthening immunization education for practicing pediatricians and trainees. Data suggest this improves the confidence of healthcare providers to discuss vaccines with parents and patients, which subsequently increases vaccination rates. One pilot study of 45 pediatric residents examining an intervention of an immersive virtual reality curriculum to educate residents on how to address vaccine hesitancy demonstrated a decreased rate of influenza vaccination refusal among patients cared for by residents who received vaccine hesitancy training compared to controls (27.8% vs 37.1%, P = .03). Additionally, the American Board of Pediatrics general pediatrics certification exam consists of 24 domains, with the first domain, Preventive Pediatrics/Well-Child Care, making up 12% of the exam. Specifically in this domain is the topic of immunizations, which includes vaccine hesitancy. In contrast, adult medicine specialties lag. The American Board of Internal Medicine internal medicine and pulmonary disease certification exams have less than 2% of questions directed toward immunization. Data on immunization education specifically for pulmonary trainees are sparse but given the vulnerability to infectious diseases in patients with pulmonary disease, effective immunization dialogue is an essential and life-saving competence for pulmonary disease specialists. In 2022 and 2023, the CDC reported that chronic lower respiratory diseases and COVID-19 were among the top 10 leading causes of death. Recognizing that vaccination in this population is a priority, the Council of Medical Specialty Societies and the CDC are funding the American Thoracic Society (ATS) and 6 other professional societies with the primary aim of increasing vaccination rates in adults. The ATS Vaccine Initiative has partnered with 8 institutions to study strategies to enhance vaccination in adults specifically with respiratory disease and notably is addressing vaccine hesitancy. This is a remarkable opportunity for the ATS and other professional organizations to develop formal immunization science curricula. Structured education will also contribute to pulmonary fellows’ overall clinical competence, with the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education underscoring the mitigation of disease risk factors and communication barriers in patients with complex pulmonary disorders as key milestones. An immunization science program tailored for pulmonary trainees could be modeled after the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society’s Comprehensive Vaccine Education Program and administered via asynchronous online modules with possible clinic-based simulation. An illustrative framework of topics could include: The history and benefits of vaccines. A review of immunology, vaccine mechanisms of action (ie, nucleic acid like messenger RNA), and ingredients (ie, adjuvants). Vaccine development and safety monitoring processes (Figure 1). Biostatistical concepts that determine vaccine efficacy. Vaccine-preventable diseases and the recommended associated vaccines for patients with respiratory disease. Examples include COVID-19, influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, pertussis, pneumococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b. Sources of vaccine hesitancy and addressing common misconceptions. Communicating vaccine recommendations: Delivering strong vaccine recommendations to patients using a presumptive format (ie, Instead of asking, “How do you feel about a pneumococcal vaccine today?,” the healthcare provider would state, “You are due to receive the pneumococcal vaccine today.”) Utilizing active listening and motivational interviewing skills for vaccine-hesitant patients such as asking open-ended questions, offering affirmations and support of autonomy, reflecting on prior patient experiences, and sharing of information. Vaccine development and licensing is overseen by the FDA’s Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research and Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee, with recommendations for use determined by the CDC’s ACIP. Abbreviations: ACIP, Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices; BEST, Biologics Effectiveness and Safety System; BLA, Biologics License Application; CDC, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; CISA, Clinical Immunization Safety Assessment; FDA, US Food and Drug Administration; IND, Investigational New Drug application; R & D, research and development; VAERS, Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System; VSD, Vaccine Safety Datalink. Dr. Osler concluded his 1914 address by appealing to the greater good but acknowledging the individual autonomy that existed in the British army stating, “It [typhoid fever] can be prevented, it must be prevented; but, meanwhile, the decision is in your hands. ...” A robust public health system provides solid footing for a flourishing society. Vaccines are vital to this, but their success ultimately requires a strong, trusting partnership between healthcare providers and the public. As healthcare educators, we need to seize the initiative to ensure our trainees are the vanguard of improvement. Supplementary Material Author contributions A.M. and B.M. equally contributed to drafting and reviewing the manuscript, providing intellectual content, and approving the final version. Supplementary material Supplementary material is available at ATS Scholar online. Conflicts of interest Please see the ICMJE disclosure forms, which have been provided as supplementary material. Funding None. Disclaimer The views expressed in this article do not communicate an official position of Luminis Health Anne Arundel Medical Center or Medstar Georgetown University Hospital. Artificial intelligence disclaimer No artificial intelligence tools were used to prepare this manuscript. papers.title: Climatic variability and routine childhood vaccine uptake in high-risk urban settlements of Karachi, Pakistan: a longitudinal fixed-effects panel analysis
papers.abstract: Climate variability may disrupt routine immunization in rapidly growing cities, where informal settlements combine high climatic exposure with fragile health services, yet longitudinal urban evidence from low- and middle-income countries is limited. We examined associations between monthly climatic conditions and routine childhood vaccine doses in 14 public and private health facilities serving nine high-risk urban union councils of Karachi, Pakistan, using 266 facility-month observations (June 2023–December 2024). Monthly doses of Bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG), pentavalent (Penta-1 to Penta-3), inactivated poliovirus (IPV-1) and measles–rubella (MR-1) vaccines were linked with reanalysis-based maximum temperature, relative humidity and wind speed, satellite-based rainfall, night-time light (NTL) and catchment population. One-way fixed-effects panel models with facility-clustered standard errors were fitted for each vaccine, with five sensitivity analyses. In the main models, wind speed was negatively associated with doses of all six vaccines (standardized β = −0.150 to −0.491), maximum temperature with five, and relative humidity positively with all six. Rainfall was negatively associated with BCG doses (β = −0.285, p < 0.001) in every specification, whereas its positive associations with Penta-2 and MR-1 did not persist after lagged climatic terms were added. The temperature association persisted only for BCG and Penta-2 when the start-up months were excluded. NTL was associated with the multi-visit doses Penta-2, Penta-3 and IPV-1. Climatic associations with routine immunization in urban informal settings therefore differ by vaccine, supporting vaccine-specific, climate-informed urban immunization planning.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 气候变化可能会扰乱快速发展的城市的常规免疫接种,这些城市的非正规住区将高气候暴露与脆弱的卫生服务结合在一起,但来自低收入和中等收入国家的纵向城市证据有限。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 提供的证据没有明确说明研究设计、设置或研究人群。
elements_zh.methods: 我们使用 266 个设施月观察数据(2023 年 6 月至 2024 年 12 月),研究了为巴基斯坦卡拉奇的 9 个高风险城市工会理事会提供服务的 14 个公共和私人卫生机构中每月气候条件与常规儿童 疫苗 剂量之间的关联。
elements_zh.main_results: NTL 与多次就诊剂量 Penta-2、Penta-3 和 IPV-1 相关。

papers.title_zh: 巴基斯坦卡拉奇高风险城市住区的气候变化和常规儿童 疫苗 吸收:纵向固定效应面板分析
papers.source_body_en: Climate variability may disrupt routine immunization in rapidly growing cities, where informal settlements combine high climatic exposure with fragile health services, yet longitudinal urban evidence from low- and middle-income countries is limited. We examined associations between monthly climatic conditions and routine childhood vaccine doses in 14 public and private health facilities serving nine high-risk urban union councils of Karachi, Pakistan, using 266 facility-month observations (June 2023–December 2024). Monthly doses of Bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG), pentavalent (Penta-1 to Penta-3), inactivated poliovirus (IPV-1) and measles–rubella (MR-1) vaccines were linked with reanalysis-based maximum temperature, relative humidity and wind speed, satellite-based rainfall, night-time light (NTL) and catchment population. One-way fixed-effects panel models with facility-clustered standard errors were fitted for each vaccine, with five sensitivity analyses. In the main models, wind speed was negatively associated with doses of all six vaccines (standardized β = −0.150 to −0.491), maximum temperature with five, and relative humidity positively with all six. Rainfall was negatively associated with BCG doses (β = −0.285, p < 0.001) in every specification, whereas its positive associations with Penta-2 and MR-1 did not persist after lagged climatic terms were added. The temperature association persisted only for BCG and Penta-2 when the start-up months were excluded. NTL was associated with the multi-visit doses Penta-2, Penta-3 and IPV-1. Climatic associations with routine immunization in urban informal settings therefore differ by vaccine, supporting vaccine-specific, climate-informed urban immunization planning.

papers.title: Overview of Health Status among Roma Population in Romania: A Scoping Review
papers.abstract: Background: Roma are widely recognized as Europe ‘s largest ethnic minority and in-dependent estimates suggest that up to two million people live in Romania. Despite well-documented socioeconomic disadvantage, no prior review has synthesized evi-dence on the health status of Roma in Romania. Objectives: This scoping review mapped the literature on healthcare access, quality of life, chronic disease burden and communicable disease exposure among Roma communities in Romania. Methods: Us-ing the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we con-ducted a systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Science Direct and supplemented by grey literature and reference-list screening, for studies published 2010–2025 in English or Romanian. Results: Thirty-nine sources (35 studies and 4 in-stitutional reports) met the inclusion criteria. Roma communities experience a life-expectancy gap of 3.5–4.6 years, markedly lower preventive-care uptake (39% vs 71% in the general population), and high rates of being uninsured (42–59%). Chronic disease burden was substantially higher than in the general population: hypertension prevalence ranged 33–67%, type 2 diabetes from 10–29%, and obesity from 32–62%, with evidence of earlier onset and more severe complications, including higher pro-gression to chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease. Health-related quality of life and mental health indicators were uniformly worse among Roma. Evidence on communicable diseases was sparse but suggested elevated hepatitis B/C prevalence and greater severity of measles and COVID-19. Conclusions: Roma communities in Romania experience markedly poorer health outcomes across nearly all domains ex-amined, driven by intersecting socioeconomic, structural and behavioral determinants.

papers.abstract_zh: 背景:罗姆人被广泛认为是欧洲最大的少数民族,独立估计表明,罗马尼亚有多达 200 万人居住。尽管有充分记录的社会经济劣势,但之前的审查尚未综合有关罗马尼亚罗姆人健康状况的证据。目标:本次范围审查绘制了有关罗马尼亚罗姆人社区医疗保健获取、生活质量、慢性疾病负担和传染病暴露的文献。方法:使用 Joanna Briggs Institute 方法和 PRISMA-ScR 指南,我们对 PubMed/MEDLINE、Web of Science、Science Direct 进行系统检索,并辅以灰色文献和参考文献列表筛选,查找 2010-2025 年以英语或罗马尼亚语发表的研究。结果:39 个来源(35 项研究和 4 项机构报告)符合纳入标准。罗姆人社区的预期寿命差距为 3.5-4.6 年,预防性护理的接受率明显较低(普通人群为 39%,普通人群为 71%),而没有保险的比例很高(42-59%)。慢性病负担显着高于普通人群:高血压 患病率 为 33-67%,2 型糖尿病为 10-29%,肥胖为 32-62%,有证据表明发病更早,并发症更严重,包括更容易进展为慢性肾病和终末期肾病。罗姆人与健康相关的生活质量和心理健康指标均较差。关于传染病的证据很少,但表明乙型/丙型肝炎 麻疹 升高,麻疹 和 COVID-19 的严重程度更高。结论:在交叉的社会经济、结构和行为决定因素的推动下,罗马尼亚的罗姆人社区在几乎所有检查领域的健康状况均明显较差。

papers.full_text: nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2356 | 2356 The enlarging scope and globalization of vaccine hesitancy By Peter Hotez As bad as it’s been, antivaccine activism is expected to worsen as it spreads from the USA to Europe and reaches into other fields of biomedicine. D uring the COVID pandemic, anti- vaccine activism became a dan- gerous and lethal force in the USA. After COVID vaccines became widely available in early 2021, what began as a reasonable public debate about immunization mandates in the work- place took a dark and dangerous turn. Parti- san media outlets introduced Americans to a range of activist contributors and pundits who falsely discredited the effectiveness and safety of mRNA vaccines. Among their false claims: mRNA vaccines would integrate into your genome and cause turbo cancers; and vaccinations were dangerous for your heart, ignoring the scientific data showing it was the SARS-CoV-2 virus inducing thromboembolic events causing heart attacks and strokes1. A vast disinformation campaign convinced hun- dreds of thousands of Americans to eschew COVID vaccines in favor of anti-parasitic drugs such as ivermectin. The consequences were deadly, with at least 200,000 unvaccinated Americans dying between mid-2021 and 2022. Health policy analyst Charles Gaba was among the first to analyze mortality data and find that deaths among unvaccinated Americans disproportionately followed a partisan divide, by a striking margin. Anti- vaccine activism became a cornerstone for ideologically driven politicians, including those tied to a wellness and influencer indus- try promoting medications or supplements of unproven benefit. Even after the human cost of vaccine refusal became clear, there was no self-reflection or course correction. The wellness industry doubled down, promoting anti-parasitic drugs as a cancer cures. In early 2025, antivaccine activism spilled over to childhood immunizations. A major measles outbreak spread from West Texas2 into neighboring states, causing dozens of hospital- izations and two deaths among unvaccinated children. In February 2025, Robert F. Kennedy Jr was sworn in as US Health Secretary, coinciding with the launch of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) Commission. He quicklu pub- licly discredited the measles–mumps–rubella (MMR) vaccine, falsely claiming it was a “leaky” vaccine contaminated with aborted fetal rem- nants, that immunity declined by 4.5% annu- ally, and that it was linked to autism. He aligned himself with wellness influencers by endors- ing a cocktail of clarithromycin, vitamin A and budesonide, then dismissed the CDC’s Advi- sory Committee on Immunization Practices and replaced its members with less-qualified individuals. In the meantime, two further mea- sles epidemics erupted in the US Southwest and South Carolina to threaten America’s elimi- nation status. In April 2026, the US Defense Secretary ended annual flu vaccine require- ments for most service members but reversed the decision after a fatal influenza outbreak at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland. MAHA disinformation continues to expand into new areas of biomedicine, promoting out- landish claims about fluoride in drinking water, the benefits of raw milk, the risks of electro- magnetic fields, and even the origins of Lyme disease. Autism remains a particular focus, extending beyond debunked vaccine claims to controversial statements about autistic indi- viduals and proposals for autism registries. These narratives largely ignore extensive evi- dence linking hundreds of autism-associated genes to neurodevelopment3, and their interactions with known risk factors includ- ing prenatal, valproic acid exposure4. As a pediatrician vaccine scientist, and parent of an adult a daughter with autism and intellec- tual disabilities5, I find the MAHA rhetoric and disregard for evidence deeply concerning. So where is this headed? In addition to DHHS’ ongoing efforts to dismantle US vac- cine policy built over decades, their actions attest to a greater MAHA aspiration — namely to build a parallel universe of alternative medi- cine aligned with the wellness industry. The strategy relies on undermining confidence in mainstream biomedicine while cutting or redi- recting government support for their specific projects. The 1910 Flexner Report exposed the weaknesses of sectarian medical schools teaching homeopathic and eclectic medicine, and helped drive the rise of scientific medicine and modern academic medical centres. Johns Hopkins Medical School was held up as the gold standard. That model has stood the test of time. Tragically, however, MAHA aspires to resurrect sectarianism in its new twenty-first century wellness incarnation. Another worry is the spread of MAHA pseu- doscience to Europe. Adoption of MAHA mes- saging by some politicians and media, along with the launch of a ‘Make Europe Healthy Again’ initiative, raises the possibility of a USA– EU alignment on MAHA-style health policies. As both regions face growing public health threats, including future pandemics and the ongoing Ebola epidemic, a return to ideologi- cally driven or pre-scientific approaches to medicine would be a major setback. papers.title: A decade of infectious disease trends in Northern Cyprus, 2014–2024
papers.abstract: Background Longitudinal infectious-disease surveillance is difficult to interpret when case definitions, diagnostic practices, and reporting structures change over time. Northern Cyprus remains underrepresented in multi-disease surveillance literature. We therefore reconstructed and harmonized official notifiable-disease data to characterize major temporal patterns while preserving epidemiologic comparability. Methods A retrospective ecological time-series analysis was conducted using official Ministry of Health surveillance records for major notifiable infections from 2014 to 2025. The primary analytical period was 2014–2024, with 2025 retained descriptively. Disease indicators were harmonized using predefined clinical and epidemiologic rules, while non-equivalent categories were analyzed within separate reporting eras. Official Statistical Institute data were used for independent cross-validation of selected annual totals and for population denominators. Notification rates per 100,000 were calculated for 2019–2024, and formal modeling was restricted to sufficiently stable series. Results Disease patterns were heterogeneous. Several infections remained sparse, whereas measles showed episodic activity with renewed notifications after 2022. Varicella fluctuated substantially, with no significant monotonic trend after adjustment for overdispersion (NRR 0.844, 95% CI 0.664–1.074; p = 0.169). Tuberculosis showed the strongest recent signal, rising from 0.44 per 100,000 in 2022 to 13.42 in 2023 and remaining elevated at 9.32 in 2024. Viral hepatitis and HIV/STI patterns were strongly influenced by surveillance-definition changes. Conclusion Notifiable infections in Northern Cyprus showed distinct temporal patterns, including episodic vaccine-preventable disease activity, continued notification of blood-borne and sexually transmitted infections, and a marked recent tuberculosis signal. To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive harmonized multi-disease analysis of official surveillance in Northern Cyprus, providing an important epidemiologic baseline for an underrepresented Eastern Mediterranean setting. Stable case definitions, compatible denominators, and stronger laboratory linkage are essential for distinguishing true epidemiologic change from reporting effects and supporting targeted public-health action.

papers.full_text: nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2363–2365 | 2363 The European Vaccines Hub Rino Rappuoli, Isabelle Bekeredjian-Ding, Pierre Van Damme, James P. Di Santo, Donata Medaglini & Michel Pletschette The European Vaccines Hub is a novel design consortium that assembles leading European organizations involved in vaccine development. The mission is to develop vaccines and monoclonal antibodies ensuring Europe’s pandemics and emerging infections readiness. When the COVID-19 pandemic struck the European Union, it was insufficiently prepared to face the devastating health and economic emergency. Although European biotech contributed significantly to the development of vaccines with products such as Comirnaty, the mRNA vaccine developed by the German BioNTech was eventually licensed to and commercialized by an American company, meaning that very few European medical countermeasures reached the market at the peak of the pandemic. A further weakness identified was that Europe did not partici- pate in any of the pivotal efficacy trials leading to licensure. To address this situation, the European Commission established the Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority (HERA) as one of its Directorates General, with the mission of strengthening the European Union’s ability to respond to major health threats through coordination, expertise and the development and procurement of medical countermeasures (MCMs). In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, HERA published a call for proposals for the creation of a European Hub for vaccine development, with the mission of developing, assessing and manufacturing vaccines for priority pathogens with epidemic and pandemic potential to ensure that Europe would be more resilient through increased preparedness. This new entity was designed to be not another institution, but rather a newly created network of existing organizations already funded by their member states to develop vaccines. The mandate of the European Vaccines Hub for Pandemic Readiness (EVH) was to create a hub able to develop and deliver vaccines end-to-end, from discovery to manufacturing. To achieve this, the EVH was expected to be organ- ized in an agile manner, allowing it to make quick decisions and to include and engage with any group from industry, biotech or academia that could contribute to development of vaccines and monoclonal antibodies against pathogens with pandemic risk. Unique new structure The EVH consortium selected for funding enabled the creation of an innovative organization that has the expertise and facilities to provide the European Union with self-sustainable and independent ability to discover, develop, assess and manufacture vaccines and antibodies against infectious diseases of epidemic and pandemic potential. This organization is based on four pillars (Fig. 1). Pillar 1 leads vaccines and monoclonal antibody discovery while advancing platforms to develop vaccines based on protein and adjuvants, on mRNA or on viral vectors. Pillar 2 drives preclinical studies to support the discovery, charac- terization and development of vaccines and monoclonal antibodies. Pillar 3 coordinates clinical development, which includes the readiness to perform ad hoc phase 1 and 2 studies and controlled human challenge studies (CHIM), with the overarching goals of putting together a network of European vaccine clinical trial centers under consented protocols and preparing to conduct large-scale phase 3 studies in collaboration with the EU ‘BE READY NOW’ project. In pillar 4, the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) and the Center for Pandemic Vaccines and Therapeutics (ZEPAI) oversee regulatory coordination and planning of manufacturing of small-scale Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) lots for early clinical studies, as well as large-scale manufacturing of final products. Although the primary scope of the EVH is to develop and build the capacity to deliver medical countermeasures, it is designed as an open organization that reaches out and engages with small and large vaccine manufacturers, biotech, academic groups, R&D units of pharmaceuti- cal companies, and projects and networks funded by European Union, for example through the Horizon Europe program. To achieve this, the EVH is following two noteworthy paths: the creation of an innovative public–private partnership model with industry and the promotion of ‘expression of interest’ calls for experts and specific projects, enabling the EVH to liaise with experts and collaborating centers that share a similar mission, both within and outside the European Union. The arrows below each pillar in Fig. 1 denote the continuous interchange between the EVH and the European system. The initial priority pathogens identified were avian influ- enza, in particular H5N1, and monkeypox (mpox). EVH activities include building the preparedness system and testing it. Indeed, the EVH’s mission creates a system that allows continuous delivery and regular updates for priorities. A living EU Epidemic and Pandemic Vaccine Readiness Plan agreed to with HERA generates an agile basis for EU pandemic preparedness. One year after the EVH was established, each of the four pillars has initiated a variety of projects and delivered important results. Pillar 1 discovered a potent and broadly protective monoclonal anti- body against mpox that recognizes a vaccine antigen not previously known to induce neutralizing antibodies. In vivo and in vitro studies in collaboration with pillar 2 confirmed that the mpox monoclonal antibody and the vaccine antigen are protective in vivo and are good candidates for continued MCM development. Pillar 3 has designed and fully enrolled a clinical trial to study the vaccine response of the European population to primary and booster immunization against the avian influenza H5N1, and is currently assessing its outcome. In the trial, H5N1-naive participants and participants immunized in 2006 with a H5N1 vaccine received an adjuvanted vaccine against the current Astrakhan clade. The study has the additional scope to establish a study cohort whose peripheral blood cells can be used to discover broadly neutralizing antibodies that recognize epitopes shared between the 2006 and 2026 H5N1 strains. Pillar 4 is addressing important bottlenecks in preparedness by mapping the European GMP facilities ready to manufacture vaccines and monoclonals for small-scale clinical trials and developing concepts for rapid ramp-up to large-scale manufacturing in pandemic crises. Its regulatory experts are addressing the anticipated practical and scientific regulatory questions required for accelerating development of EVH products to enable early availability of products. In addition, the EVH has initiated collaborations with external entities. One involves joint participation with Sanofi, a major Euro- pean vaccine manufacturer, in an EU tender to develop a mucosal mRNA vaccine against the H5N1 avian influenza. Another involves the publication of an ‘expression of interest’ to identify possible col- laborators that can contribute to further pandemic influenza vaccine development approaches. Stress testing While the EVH was working on setting up its organization, two unex- pected, highly lethal emerging infections were communicated by the World Health Organization in May 2026. The first was the Andes hanta- virus outbreak, reported on 2 May, involving a cruise ship coming out of Argentina1, and the second was the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda that was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on 17 May2. Although these were not imminent threats for Europe, after rapid consultation with HERA, it was agreed that it would be important for Europe to par- ticipate in the development of countermeasures for these viruses. The question was whether the EVH had the capacity to address these two targets that, up to that moment, had never been considered. Consultation of the EVH network identified a broadly protective human monoclonal antibody against Andes hantavirus discovered in a Swedish patient infected with Puumala hantavirus, which had been characterized by several German academic groups and whose structure had been determined a few years ago at the Institut Pasteur in Paris3. This antibody had been acquired and improved by two US R&D enterprises but was never brought into clinical development. Concurrently, the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) labora- tories revealed recent results identifying a potent human monoclonal antibody that neutralizes both Ebola Zaire and Ebola Bundibugyo. The antibody had been shown to protect mice from challenge with the virus in the Biosafety Level 4 (BSL4) facility in Marburg4. As such, in less than a month, the two antibodies were selected by the EVH for development up to clinical testing. For antibody expression, EVH is developing an innovative platform based on the C1 fungus, which is expected to enable cost-effective production of large quantities of monoclonal antibodies, making these therapies more accessible to at-risk populations and to low-income countries at an affordable and equitable cost5. The stress test arising from the unexpected outbreaks showed that the EVH can leverage the ad hoc development of a multitude of innova- tive prototypes from excellent European entities that have hitherto failed to translate them into products when working in isolation. The EVH can turn these product candidates into countermeasures to protect people’s health. Moreover, the EVH network had at its disposal two vac- cine prototypes for the development of an Ebola vaccine: an MVA-based vaccine against Ebola Zaire developed by DZIF-associated EVH mem- bers, previously shown to be protective in a mouse challenge study performed at the Marburg BSL-4 facility6, and a measles vector-based pan-filovirus vaccine in development at the Institut Pasteur. Once added to the EVH portfolio, these projects could become highly relevant in the race against Bundibugyo virus. Furthermore, monoclonal antibodies candidates could provide an important complementary strategy, with the advantage of providing immediate protection. Looking to the future In conclusion, the EVH is an organization rooting pandemic prepar- edness within an innovative cross-sectorial ecosystem, which in its first year of existence has shown the potential to deliver innovative countermeasures. We can probably describe the EVH as both a dis- covery and development engine and a catalyst able to aggregate the best European competencies and discoveries, transforming them into medical products that include vaccines and monoclonal antibodies. The big question is whether the EVH will be able to exploit this poten- tial and deliver real products. There are numerous challenges that could interfere with this ambitious goal. One of the most important limitations is the fact that the products in the EVH portfolio do not have an immediate attractive commercial market value because they address infectious diseases that are rare, or pandemics that we hope will never happen. The absence of immediate commercial value, com- monly defined as a market failure, is a recurrent problem for most medical countermeasures. In the absence of an expected immediate and secure return on investment, the private sector is little inclined to start rapid development and manufacturing programs. Notwithstand- ing that complication, the instruments developed by the EU in terms of stockpiling essential and possibly innovative MCMs and the constant readiness of the reality-tested joint procurement mechanism are robust attempts to provide solutions to these problems. Although we have the technology to develop effective products against most infectious diseases, these need to become available for wide implementation despite the absence of immediate pre- dictable markets. It is therefore important to address, on a global scale, the longer-term sustainability of MCM development, which can be clearly seen to be an insurance for the health and economic security of every country, and to move out of the disastrous cycle of panic and neglect. nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2363–2365 | 2365 Comment Rino Rappuoli 1,2 , Isabelle Bekeredjian-Ding1,3,4, Pierre Van Damme 1,5, James P. papers.title: Closing Somalia’s childhood vaccination gap in the digital era: a perspective on misinformation, trust, and access
papers.abstract: Somalia’s childhood immunization coverage has improved, but important gaps remain across vaccine doses, populations, and places. The latest WHO/UNICEF estimates for 2025 report 77% coverage for the first dose of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis-containing vaccine (DTP1), 72% for DTP3, and 61% for the first measles-containing vaccine (MCV1), while the 2020 Somali Health and Demographic Survey documented far lower household-survey coverage. These measures are not directly interchangeable and illustrate both progress and continuing uncertainty in a fragile data environment. This Perspective argues that misinformation, trust, and access should be examined together, while recognizing that Somalia-specific evidence on digital vaccine misinformation remains limited. Established WHO Behavioural and Social Drivers of vaccination (BeSD) and WHO/UNICEF social-listening guidance are therefore adapted into an operational pathway for Somalia rather than presented as a new behavioral theory. The adaptation specifies responsible actors, offline and digital listening channels, linguistic and data-system requirements, service-linkage rules, safeguards for conflict settings, and an evaluation strategy. A preferred evaluation would use phased matched-district implementation with DTP3 coverage as the primary outcome, complemented by zero-dose, timeliness, missed-opportunity, responsiveness, and equity indicators. Digital listening should be treated as one sentinel input among community and service data, not as a population-representative measure. The public health value of the pathway ultimately depends on whether verified concerns are translated into trusted communication and reachable vaccination services, especially for displaced, nomadic, insecure, and digitally excluded communities.

papers.abstract_zh: 索马里的儿童免疫覆盖率有所提高,但 疫苗 剂量、人群和地点之间仍存在重要差距。世卫组织/联合国儿童基金会对 2025 年的最新估计报告称,首剂含白喉-破伤风-百日咳的 疫苗 (DTP1) 覆盖率为 77%,DTP3 为 72%,首剂含 麻疹 (MCV1) 的覆盖率为 61%,而 2020 年索马里健康和人口调查记录的覆盖率要低得多家庭调查覆盖范围。这些措施不能直接互换,它们说明了脆弱数据环境中的进展和持续的不确定性。本观点认为,错误信息、信任和获取应一起审查,同时认识到索马里有关数字 疫苗 错误信息的具体证据仍然有限。因此,既定的世卫组织 疫苗接种 (BeSD) 行为和社会驱动因素和世卫组织/联合国儿童基金会社会倾听指南被改编为索马里的操作途径,而不是作为新的行为理论提出。该改编规定了负责任的参与者、离线和数字收听渠道、语言和数据系统要求、服务链接规则、冲突设置的保障措施以及评估策略。首选的评估将采用分阶段匹配区实施,以 DTP3 覆盖率作为主要结果,并辅以零剂量、及时性、错失机会、响应性和公平性指标。数字聆听应被视为社区和服务数据中的一个哨兵输入,而不是一种具有人口代表性的措施。该途径的公共卫生价值最终取决于经过验证的担忧是否转化为可信的沟通和可达的 疫苗接种 服务,特别是对于流离失所、游牧、不安全和数字排斥的社区。

papers.full_text: nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2355 | 2355 Vaccinology 2.0 The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the success of vaccine development, but more improvements in vaccine design, equity, manufacturing and changes in public health policy are warranted. O ne of the global health success stories has been the develop­ ment of vaccines. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), we now have vaccines to more than 30 life-threatening infections, which is estimated to prevent 3.5 million to 5 million deaths every year. The recent COVID-19 pandemic showcased vaccine development at its best. Vaccines against SARS-CoV-2 were developed at record speed, facilitated by new technologies such as the mRNA vaccine platform and spurred by the wealth of existing knowledge of virology, vac­ cinology and structural biology. However, much has changed since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. In this issue of Nature Immunology, we have commissioned several commentaries from experts across the globe that collectively summarize recent progress and discuss the challenges faced in this field. Although the COVID-19 pandemic high­ lighted the transformative potential of mRNA platforms, gaps remain for global pandemic preparedness according to Florian Kram­ mer. In his Comment, Krammer argues that there is a need to advance mucosal vaccines to improve protection against respiratory infection and transmission, and to develop more broadly protective vaccines that target entire virus families. In addition, strengthen­ ing regulatory policy and sustaining support for basic research on emerging pathogens is needed. However, the current US adminis­ tration has adopted measures that weaken vaccine development in the USA by the deci­ sion to withdraw federal support for mRNA vaccine development. This action led to the cancellation of research grant contracts worth approximately US$500 million, affecting ongoing mRNA therapeutic projects involv­ ing universities, research institutes and major pharmaceutical companies. In addition to funding cuts, the public health policies of the current US government are promoting vaccine hesitancy. In a World View article, Peter Hotez argues that the rise of the US Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement has weakened confidence in evidence-based medicine, contributed to out­ breaks of vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles, and fostered efforts to replace established scientific and regulatory frame­ works with wellness-oriented ideologies. Wor­ ryingly, vaccine hesitancy has evolved from a movement focused on COVID-19 vaccines into a broader anti-science campaign that increas­ ingly shapes public health policy, promotes misinformation and extends to areas such as childhood immunization, autism, fluoride, raw milk and alternative medicine. Further­ more, Hotez warns that these trends are spreading internationally, particularly into Europe, raising concerns that growing accept­ ance of pseudoscientific health policies could undermine pandemic preparedness, biomedi­ cal research and public health outcomes on a global scale. On a more optimistic note, in their Com­ ment Michael J. Hogan and Norbert Pardi discuss advances across other RNA technolo­ gies that aim to improve efficacy, reduce reac­ togenicity and enhance T cell and mucosal immune responses. A deeper understanding of RNA and lipid-nanoparticle biology, com­ bined with innovations in delivery systems and immune modulation, is still needed to engi­ neer vaccines that produce different types of immune response depending on the disease being treated. Similarly, the COVID-19 pan­ demic exposed the vulnerability of Africa and other lower-income regions to dependence on external vaccine suppliers. Shabir A. Madhi and Glenda E. Gray state in their Comment that the local manufacturing of routine vaccines in Africa is often economically uncompeti­ tive and may divert resources from broader public health goals. Instead, they advocate for strategic investment in adaptable vaccine platforms such as mRNA and viral-vector technologies, outbreak-response manufac­ turing capacity, regulatory expertise, clini­ cal development infrastructure and skilled workforce development. In their Comment, Rino Rappuoli et al. high­ light the European Vaccines Hub for Pandemic Readiness (EVH) created in response to short­ comings exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic. The EVH is designed to strengthen pandemic preparedness by integrating vaccine and monoclonal antibody discovery, preclinical and clinical development, regulatory plan­ ning and manufacturing capabilities into a coordinated, end-to-end development net­ work. The initiative aims to translate Europe’s strong scientific base into deployable medi­ cal countermeasures for emerging infectious diseases and is currently focusing on threats such as H5N1 influenza. The authors highlight EVH’s early achievements, including the iden­ tification of promising vaccine and antibody candidates, the establishment of clinical trial infrastructure, and rapid responses to emerging threats, such as Andes hantavirus and Ebola Bundibugyo outbreaks. Finally, in his Comment, Bali Pulendran looks at the future of vaccine research by pointing out the vaccine-induced protection extends beyond antibody and T cell responses to encompass a broader spectrum of ‘protec­ tive immune states’ within tissues, in which coordinated networks of immune and non­ immune cells confer heightened resistance to infection. Recent studies of intravenous BCG and mucosal vaccination suggest that protection can emerge from coordinated interactions among adaptive immune cells, innate cells and structural cells within tissues. These interactions create organ-embedded states of increased resistance that provide broad protection against diverse pathogens, a phenomenon termed ‘integrated organ immu­ nity’. Pulendran proposes that future vacci­ nology should shift from focusing primarily on antigens and immune correlates toward identifying, characterizing and deliberately engineering these protective immune states, potentially enabling more durable and broadly protective vaccines against infectious diseases and other immune-mediated conditions. This ‘Vaccinology 2.0’ focus highlights the achievements of vaccine research in the past 6 years and showcases issues that still need to be tackled to ensure the continued development, improvement and accessibility of vaccines for future generations and ensure that we are prepared for the next pandemic. papers.title: A RARE CASE OF ACUTE IMMUNE THROMBOCYTOPENIC PURPURA TEMPORALLY ASSOCIATED WITH ROUTINE TWO-MONTH IMMUNIZATION.
papers.abstract: Background: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is one of the causes of platelet deficiency. Although vaccinations, particularly MMR, have been reported as a potential temporal trigger, ITP following routine infant immunisation is very rare. Case Summary: We describe the case of a previously healthy 2-month-old infant who was brought to the Emergency Department by his parents with complaints of a spreading non-blanching petechial rash and bruising, which started three days back, initially more prominent over the legs and later on spreading towards the chest. The baby was born at full term by spontaneous vaginal delivery requiring vacuum assistance and no bleeding and bruising were observed at the time of delivery and he didn’t require any admission at the time of birth. The baby on presentation was clinically well, was tolerating oral feeds, there was no history of fever, and no history of preceding viral illness; there was also no history of any trauma. Of note, the infant received his routine childhood vaccinations, including 6 in 1, PCV, Men B, and oral rotavirus 15 days ago. The mother also noted bruising and swelling at the Men B injection site. Method: Upon arrival to the ED after a detailed history, blood tests were done, and initial investigations demonstrated isolated severe thrombocytopenia, with a platelet count of 6 × 109/L, hemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL, and white blood cell count of 9.4 × 109/L. Blood film showed thrombocytopenia with no evidence of platelet clumping noted. The initial film showed neutropenia with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.74 x 109/L and occasional reactive lymphocytes. No blast cells were seen. Coagulation studies were also done and were normal. His cranial ultrasonography was also reported as normal. The extended respiratory viral panel was negative, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus testing were negative as well. The patient was then discussed with the paeds hematology team and a diagnosis of acute immune thrombocytopenia was made. Considering the really low platelet count, it was planned to give IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin), and the infant received one dose of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). The patient remained stable afterward, and repeat FBC (full blood count) showed an improving trend in the platelet count; as the platelet count started to improve, hematology advised discharging him and doing weekly platelet counts. Platelet counts improved to 68 × 109/L two weeks after treatment and subsequently normalised to 508 × 109/L at five months' follow-up. Routine immunisations were temporarily deferred until platelet recovery and were later resumed according to the national immunisation schedule. The family was also reassured that future measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination was not contraindicated. Conclusion: This case highlights the importance of recognizing ITP in an otherwise well-appearing child who presents with bruising and petechiae with a blood film showing isolated thrombocytopenia. It is also important that we exclude other alternative causes and promptly treat ITP with IVIG after discussion with the hematology team. Also, close haematology follow-up resulted in complete platelet recovery and safe resumption of routine childhood immunisations.

Blood film showed thrombocytopenia with no evidence of platelet clumping noted. The initial film showed neutropenia with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.74 x 109/L and occasional reactive lymphocytes. No blast cells were seen. Coagulation studies were also done and were normal. His cranial ultrasonography was also reported as normal. The extended respiratory viral panel was negative, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus testing were negative as well. The patient was then discussed with the paeds hematology team and a diagnosis of acute immune thrombocytopenia was made. Considering the really low platelet count, it was planned to give IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin), and the infant received one dose of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). The patient remained stable afterward, and repeat FBC (full blood count) showed an improving trend in the platelet count; as the platelet count started to improve, hematology advised discharging him and doing weekly platelet counts. Platelet counts improved to 68 × 109/L two weeks after treatment and subsequently normalised to 508 × 109/L at five months' follow-up. Routine immunisations were temporarily deferred until platelet recovery and were later resumed according to the national immunisation schedule. The family was also reassured that future measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination was not contraindicated. Conclusion: This case highlights the importance of recognizing ITP in an otherwise well-appearing child who presents with bruising and petechiae with a blood film showing isolated thrombocytopenia. It is also important that we exclude other alternative causes and promptly treat ITP with IVIG after discussion with the hematology team. Also, close haematology follow-up resulted in complete platelet recovery and safe resumption of routine childhood immunisations.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景:免疫性血小板减少性紫癜是血小板缺乏的原因之一。尽管 疫苗接种,特别是 MMR,已被报道为潜在的时间触发因素,但常规婴儿免疫接种后的 ITP 非常罕见。病例摘要:我们描述了一名先前健康的 2 个月大婴儿的病例,他被父母带到急诊室,抱怨三天前开始出现扩散的非变白的点状皮疹和瘀伤,最初在腿部更加突出,后来向胸部蔓延。婴儿足月出生,通过自然阴道分娩,需要真空辅助,分娩时没有观察到出血和瘀伤,出生时不需要任何入院。就诊的婴儿临床表现良好,能够耐受经口喂养,没有发烧史,也没有既往病毒性疾病史;也没有任何外伤史。值得注意的是,该婴儿于 15 天前接受了童年常规 疫苗接种,包括 6 合 1、PCV、Men B 和口服轮状病毒。这位母亲还注意到 Men B 注射部位有瘀伤和肿胀。方法:在详细询问病史后到达急诊室后,进行了血液检查,初步检查显示孤立性严重血小板减少症,血小板计数为 6 × 109/L,血红蛋白为 10.5 g/dL,白细胞计数为 9.4 × 109/L。血涂片显示血小板减少,没有发现血小板聚集的证据。最初的胶片显示中性粒细胞减少症,中性粒细胞绝对计数为 0.74 x 109/L,偶尔有反应性淋巴细胞。没有看到母细胞。还进行了凝血研究,结果正常。他的颅骨超声检查也报告为正常。扩展呼吸道病毒检测结果呈阴性,爱泼斯坦-巴尔病毒和巨细胞病毒检测也呈阴性。随后与 paeds 血液学团队对该患者进行了讨论,并制定了急性免疫性血小板减少症的 诊断。考虑到血小板计数确实较低,计划给予IVIG(静脉注射免疫球蛋白),婴儿接受了一剂静脉注射免疫球蛋白(IVIG)。此后患者病情稳定,复查FBC(全血细胞计数)显示血小板计数有改善趋势;随着血小板计数开始改善,血液学建议他出院并每周进行血小板计数。治疗 两周后血小板计数改善至 68 × 109/L,随后在五个月的随访中正常化至 508 × 109/L。常规免疫接种暂时推迟至血小板恢复后,随后根据国家免疫接种计划恢复。家人也放心,未来的 麻疹、腮腺炎和风疹 (MMR) 疫苗接种 没有禁忌症。结论:该病例强调了识别 ITP 的重要性,该儿童在其他方面表现良好,但出现瘀伤和瘀点,血涂片显示孤立性血小板减少症。同样重要的是,我们要排除其他替代原因,并在与血液学团队讨论后立即使用 IVIG 治疗 ITP。此外,密切的血液学随访导致血小板完全恢复并安全恢复常规儿童免疫接种。

papers.title: National and Regional Trends in Childhood Vaccination Coverage in Türkiye, 1985–2025: An Ecological Time Series Study
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: National averages may conceal regional declines in childhood vaccination. I described trends in administrative coverage published for Türkiye and its regions through 2025. Methods: Coverage of the third diphtheria–pertussis–tetanus dose (DPT3), BCG, third hepatitis B dose (HBV3), first measles-containing dose (MCV1) and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) was extracted from Ministry of Health publications. Joinpoint regression with Bonferroni adjustment was applied to the 12 NUTS-1 regions for 2002–2025 and repeated for 2009–2025, 2019–2025 and alternative specifications. Results: In 2025, national coverage was 94% for DPT3, 93% for BCG and 92% for MCV1 and the PCV booster. Regional indicators rose steeply until joinpoints in 2006–2012, years that overlap schedule and reporting changes. Later slopes were mostly negative; in the principal models, six DPT3 or MCV1 declines met the adjusted threshold in 2009–2025, all in Central Anatolia, Western Anatolia and the Black Sea regions, and none in the other windows. MCV1 declines in Central Anatolia and Western Black Sea persisted under every specification. BCG declined in the same regions; all PCV booster slopes were negative, none meeting the threshold. Units reporting at least 95% coverage fell from 80 to 32 of 81 for DPT3 and from 75 to 19 for MCV1 during 2013–2025; the 2018 survey DPT3 estimate was 19 points below the administrative value. Conclusions: Published coverage has plateaued and, in central and Black Sea regions, declined slowly, most consistently for MCV1. Its link to true uptake is uncertain. Active recall in these regions, a national coverage survey and a denominator audit are needed.

elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 这些地区需要积极召回、全国范围调查和分母审计。

papers.abstract_zh: 背景/目标:全国平均水平可能掩盖了儿童 疫苗接种 的区域下降。我描述了截至 2025 年土耳其及其地区发布的行政覆盖范围的趋势。方法:白喉-百日咳-破伤风第三剂 (DPT3)、卡介苗、乙型肝炎第三剂 (HBV3)、含 麻疹 的第一剂 (MCV1) 和肺炎球菌结合物 疫苗 (PCV) 的覆盖范围摘自卫生部出版物。结合 Bonferroni 调整的连接点回归应用于 2002-2025 年的 12 个 NUTS-1 区域,并在 2009-2025 年、2019-2025 年和替代规范中重复。结果:到 2025 年,DPT3 的全国覆盖率为 94%,BCG 的全国覆盖率为 93%,MCV1 和 PCV 加强疫苗的全国覆盖率为 92%。区域指标急剧上升,直到 2006 年至 2012 年的连接点,这些年份与时间表和报告变化重叠。后来的斜率大多为负;在主要模型中,2009-2025 年有 6 次 DPT3 或 MCV1 下降达到调整后的阈值,全部位于安纳托利亚中部、安纳托利亚西部和黑海地区,其他窗口中没有一次。在各种规格下,安纳托利亚中部和黑海西部的 MCV1 持续下降。BCG 在同一地区有所下降;所有 PCV 助推器斜率均为负,没有达到阈值。2013 年至 2025 年期间,报告覆盖率至少 95% 的单位从 DPT3 的 81 个单位中的 80 个下降到 32 个,MCV1 的单位从 75 个下降到 19 个;2018 年调查 DPT3 估计值比行政值低 19 个百分点。结论:已发表的报道已趋于稳定,在中部和黑海地区,缓慢下降,MCV1 的报道最为一致。它与真实吸收率的联系尚不确定。这些地区需要积极召回、全国范围调查和分母审计。

papers.title: SAKTI: DEVELOPMENT OF AN INTEGRATED HEALTH ANALYTICS DASHBOARD TO SUPPORT DATA-DRIVEN DECISION-MAKING AT THE SLEMAN DISTRICT HEALTH OFFICE
papers.abstract: Objective: This study aimed to develop a web-based integrated health analytics dashboard prototype named SAKTI, an acronym for Sistem Analitik Kesehatan Terintegrasi (Integrated Health Analytics System), as a decision-support tool at the Sleman District Health Office. Method: The system was developed using the System Development Life Cycle (SDLC) approach with the Waterfall model, encompassing requirement analysis, system design, implementation, and initial testing. The initial dataset used in the prototype included three priority health indicators in Sleman Regency for the 2023–2025 period: dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) and measles in the Disease Prevention and Control Department, and stunting in the Public Health Department. Results: This study produced a web-based SAKTI dashboard prototype with a modular architecture designed to represent four main departments at the Sleman District Health Office: Disease Prevention and Control, Public Health, Health Services, and Health Resources. In the initial development stage, active data implementation focused on two modules—Disease Prevention and Control and Public Health—while the Health Services and Health Resources modules were prepared as integration-ready modules. The dashboard features two-factor authentication, trend charts, distribution maps, demographic visualizations, and cross-department summary tables. The resulting visualizations effectively illustrated differences in indicator dynamics, including a rise in dengue hemorrhagic fever cases, a decline in the measles positivity rate, and a decrease in stunting prevalence alongside inter-area disparities. Novelty: SAKTI serves as a proof-of-concept for an integrated health dashboard that provides an initial foundation for strengthening data-driven decision-making at the district health office level.
