analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to develop a web-based integrated health analytics dashboard named SAKTI to support data-driven decision-making at the Sleman District Health Office. The system was developed using the System Development Life Cycle (SDLC) approach with the Waterfall model, incorporating requirement analysis, system design, implementation, and initial testing. The initial dataset included three priority health indicators: dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF), measles, and stunting. The prototype dashboard features a modular architecture with four main departments represented, including Disease Prevention and Control, Public Health, Health Services, and Health Resources. It includes functionalities such as two-factor authentication, trend charts, distribution maps, demographic visualizations, and cross-department summary tables. The resulting visualizations demonstrated differences in health indicator dynamics, such as an increase in DHF cases, a decline in measles positivity rate, and a decrease in stunting prevalence. The study highlights SAKTI as a proof-of-concept for an integrated health dashboard that can strengthen data-driven decision-making at the district health office level. The evidence is based on the initial development stage and features of the dashboard, with a moderate confidence level due to the absence of detailed results and limitations.

papers.abstract_zh: 目标:本研究旨在开发一个名为 SAKTI 的基于网络的综合健康分析仪表板原型,SAKTI 是 Sistem Analitik Kesehatan Terintegrasi(综合健康分析系统)的缩写,作为 Sleman 地区卫生办公室的决策支持工具。方法:该系统是使用系统开发生命周期(SDLC)方法和瀑布模型开发的,包括需求分析、系统设计、实施和初始测试。原型中使用的初始数据集包括斯勒曼县 2023-2025 年期间的三个优先健康指标:疾病预防和控制部门的登革出血热 (DHF) 和 麻疹,以及公共卫生部门的发育迟缓。结果:本研究制作了一个基于网络的 SAKTI 仪表板原型,该原型采用模块化架构,旨在代表斯勒曼地区卫生办公室的四个主要部门:疾病预防和控制、公共卫生、卫生服务和卫生资源。在最初的开发阶段,主动数据实施主要集中在疾病预防控制和公共卫生两个模块,而卫生服务和卫生资源模块则准备为集成就绪模块。仪表板具有双因素身份验证、趋势图、分布图、人口统计可视化和跨部门汇总表。由此产生的可视化效果有效地说明了指标动态的差异,包括登革出血热病例的增加、麻疹 阳性率的下降以及发育迟缓的 麻疹 的减少以及区域间差异。新颖性:SAKTI 作为综合健康仪表板的概念验证,为加强地区卫生办公室级别的数据驱动决策奠定了初步基础。

analysis_zh.methods: 原型中使用的初始数据集包括斯勒曼县 2023-2025 年期间的三个优先健康指标:疾病预防和控制部门的登革出血热 (DHF) 和 麻疹,以及公共卫生部门的发育迟缓。
analysis_zh.main_results: 这项研究制作了一个基于网络的 SAKTI 仪表板原型,该原型具有模块化架构,旨在代表斯勒曼地区卫生办公室的四个主要部门:疾病预防和控制、公共卫生、卫生服务和卫生资源。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 仪表板具有双因素身份验证、趋势图、分布图、人口统计可视化和跨部门汇总表。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 由此产生的可视化效果有效地说明了指标动态的差异,包括登革出血热病例的增加、麻疹 阳性率的下降以及发育迟缓的 麻疹 的减少以及区域间差异。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 新颖性:SAKTI 作为综合健康仪表板的概念验证,为加强地区卫生办公室级别的数据驱动决策奠定了初步基础。

papers.title: Undernutrition among children aged 6–59 months attending Afgooye Hospital, Somalia: a facility-based cross-sectional study

source_records.title: Undernutrition among children aged 6–59 months attending Afgooye Hospital, Somalia: a facility-based cross-sectional study

papers.priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
papers.full_text: AbstractBackgroundChild undernutrition remains a major public-health problem in Somalia, where conflict, climate shocks, displacement and food insecurity strain health and WASH services. National surveys inform planning but do not describe the children who present to individual facilities. We describe anthropometric undernutrition among children aged 6–59 months attending Afgooye Hospital.MethodsIn this facility-based cross-sectional study (February–March 2025), children attending growth monitoring were recruited consecutively. Weight, length/height and mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) were measured following WHO procedures, and Z-scores were calculated with WHO Anthro using the WHO Child Growth Standards. Analysis was descriptive, with Wilson 95% confidence intervals. Displacement status was not recorded and duplicate measurements were not taken.ResultsOf 422 children, 94.3% (95% CI 91.7–96.1) were stunted (55.9% severely) and 79.9% (95% CI 75.8–83.4) were wasted by weight-for-height Z-score, whereas 39.1% (95% CI 34.6–43.8) had acute malnutrition by MUAC. Colostrum was reported for 47.6% of children, prior exclusive breastfeeding for 20.6%, and diarrhoea in the preceding two weeks for 64.5%. These estimates could not be checked against duplicate measurements and should be interpreted cautiously.ConclusionChildren attending Afgooye Hospital in this two-month period had a very high burden of anthropometric undernutrition. Because recruitment was consecutive, at one facility, in the Jilaal dry season, and without duplicate measurements, the estimates describe this clinic cohort and are not district prevalence. They support strengthened facility-based screening and care, and representative, seasonally repeated community surveillance that records displacement status.Keywords: Afgooye, child nutrition, facility-based study, MUAC, Somalia, stunting, undernutrition, wasting 2.Materials and methods2.1.Design and settingWe conducted a facility-based cross-sectional study from February to March 2025 at Afgooye Hospital, about 30 km from Mogadishu, which provides maternal and child health services including growth monitoring. The study characterizes children attending this service; it was not designed to estimate community or district prevalence.2.2.ParticipantsChildren aged 6–59 months attending the hospital for growth monitoring were eligible, and caregivers gave informed consent. Children already enrolled at an earlier visit were excluded to avoid duplicates. The study records do not specify whether children already enrolled in a nutrition programme, referred for acute malnutrition or admitted as inpatients were eligible, or whether bilateral pitting oedema was assessed; these gaps are acknowledged as limitations.2.3.Sample size and recruitmentThe single-proportion formula was used with 95% confidence, 5% absolute precision and an expected prevalence of 50% [which maximizes p(1 − p) when no reliable local estimate exists], giving 384 children; adding 10% for non-response gave a target of 422. The calculation addresses precision of a prevalence estimate, not power for association analyses. Eligible children were recruited consecutively from the clinic attendance register until 422 were enrolled. This non-probability approach may over-represent children whose caregivers sought care because of growth or health concerns, limiting generalizability.2.4.Data collectionTrained data collectors used an interviewer-administered questionnaire covering socio-demographic characteristics, feeding history, recent illness and vaccination, supplemented by review of vaccination cards and medical records. Completed questionnaires were checked daily for completeness and consistency. Food-group questions were not analysed because the questionnaire did not define a reproducible recall period or a validated dietary-diversity score. Displacement status (host community versus internally displaced) was not collected and was not inferred retrospectively; no analysis by displacement status is reported.2.5.Definitions of variablesDefinitions applied in this analysis were as follows; caregiver report was the source unless stated.Vaccination: complete if the card or caregiver report documented all doses due for the child’s age in the Somali EPI schedule (BCG, OPV0, three doses of OPV and pentavalent, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, and measles-containing vaccine from 9 months); incomplete if at least one but not all due doses were received; none if no dose was documented or reported. Assessment against age-appropriate doses prevented infants under 9 months being classed as incomplete for measles vaccine alone.Colostrum feeding: the first yellowish milk was given rather than discarded. Prior exclusive breastfeeding: only breast milk (apart from oral rehydration salts, vitamins, minerals or prescribed medicines) during the first six months of life; this is a retrospective report for children of all ages and is not equivalent to the survey indicator restricted to infants under six months. Currently breastfeeding: any breast milk at interview.Recent illness (preceding two weeks): diarrhoea was three or more loose or watery stools in 24 h; respiratory-infection symptoms were cough with short, rapid or difficult breathing attributed to a chest problem; fever was caregiver-reported and not measured. History of measles: reported clinical diagnosis at any time or documentation in the record. Deworming: albendazole or mebendazole in the previous six months, by report or record.Caregiver education: no formal education versus any formal schooling. Household income: caregiver-reported total household income in the previous month, in US dollars, categorized as below versus at or above US$100.2.6.Anthropometric measurement and data qualityMeasurements followed WHO procedures. Weight was measured to the nearest 0.1 kg on a Salter scale with the child in light clothing. Recumbent length was measured for children under 24 months and standing height with a mechanical stadiometer from 24 months. MUAC was measured with a tricolour tape Data collectors were trained, equipment was checked, and forms were reviewed daily. The source used to establish each child’s age (birth certificate, health card or caregiver recall) was not documented. Duplicate measurements and formal inter-observer standardization were not carried out.No flagged-value screening, independent re-entry of data or other formal data-quality audit was performed or documented, and Z-score distributions were not retained for this report. Prevalence estimates are therefore reported as recorded and have not been independently verified; the implications are discussed in Section 4.2.2.7.Nutritional statusHeight-for-age (HAZ) and weight-for-height (WHZ) Z-scores were calculated with WHO Anthro and the WHO Child Growth Standards. Stunting was HAZ < −2 SD (severe <−3 SD) and wasting was WHZ < −2 SD (severe <−3 SD). By MUAC, <11.5 cm indicated severe and 11.5 to <12.5 cm moderate acute malnutrition. WHZ- and MUAC-based classifications were compared at the aggregate level only.2.8.Statistical analysisData were analysed in SPSS version 26. We report counts and percentages with Wilson 95% confidence intervals. The study was not designed to identify determinants, and we did not fit regression models for three reasons: (i) only 24 children were not stunted (and 85 not wasted), so models with several covariates would be unstable and prone to sparse-data bias; (ii) the sample size was calculated for prevalence precision rather than for association analyses; and (iii) odds ratios from logistic models overstate prevalence ratios when the outcome is common, and non-random facility selection would make any such estimate hard to interpret. No p-values or adjusted estimates are presented, and statements about associated factors are not made.2.9.Ethical approvalThe Institutional Review Board of SIMAD University, Mogadishu, approved the study. Written and verbal informed consent was obtained from caregivers. Confidentiality and anonymity were maintained. 3.Results3.1.ParticipantsA total of 422 children were analysed. Counts of children screened, ineligible, declining or excluded for incomplete anthropometry were not recorded, so a participant-flow diagram cannot be provided. Most children were aged 6–11 months (38.6%) or 12–23 months (38.2%), and 55.2% were female. Most caregivers were married (69.2%), 46.4% had no formal education, and 70.4% of households reported income below US$100 per month (Table 1).Table 1Socio-demographic, feeding and recent health characteristics of children aged 6–59 months attending Afgooye Hospital, Somalia, February–March 2025 (N = 422).DomainCharacteristicn (%)Socio-demographicAge 6–11 months163 (38.6)Age 12–23 months161 (38.2)Age 24–59 months98 (23.2)Female233 (55.2)Male189 (44.8)Caregiver married292 (69.2)Caregiver widowed, divorced or separated130 (30.8)Caregiver with no formal education196 (46.4)Caregiver with any formal education226 (53.6)Household income <US$100/month297 (70.4)Household income ≥US$100/month125 (29.6)FeedingReceived colostrum201 (47.6)Did not receive colostrum221 (52.4)Previously exclusively breastfed87 (20.6)Not previously exclusively breastfed335 (79.4)Currently breastfeeding148 (35.1)Not currently breastfeeding274 (64.9)VaccinationComplete131 (31.0)Incomplete94 (22.3)None197 (46.7)Recent healthDiarrhoea, preceding two weeks272 (64.5)No diarrhoea150 (35.5)Respiratory-infection symptoms195 (46.2)No respiratory-infection symptoms227 (53.8)Fever, preceding two weeks211 (50.0)No fever211 (50.0)History of measles155 (36.7)No history of measles267 (63.3)Dewormed in previous six months121 (28.7)Not dewormed301 (71.3)Percentages are within each variable (N = 422). All feeding and health variables are caregiver-reported, verified against cards or records where available.3.2.Feeding and recent healthColostrum was reported for 47.6% (201/422) of children and prior exclusive breastfeeding for 20.6% (87/422); 35.1% (148/422) were still breastfeeding. Vaccination was complete in 31.0%, incomplete in 22.3% and absent in 46.7% (197/422). In the preceding two weeks, 64.5% (272/422) had diarrhoea, 46.2% had respiratory-infection symptoms and 50.0% had fever; 36.7% had a history of measles and 28.7% had been dewormed in the previous six months (Table 1). All these variables rely on caregiver report and are subject to recall and social-desirability bias.3.3.Nutritional statusStunting affected 94.3% (398/422; 95% CI 91.7–96.1) of children, including 55.9% with severe stunting. Wasting by WHZ affected 79.9% (337/422; 95% CI 75.8–83.4), almost all of it moderate (76.1%; severe 3.8%). By MUAC, 34.1% had moderate and 5.0% severe acute malnutrition, 39.1% (95% CI 34.6–43.8) in total, while 60.9% were normal (Table 2; Figures 1, 2). Z-score distributions, underweight, flagged values and results by age group and sex were not available for this report. These values are far above national population estimates (3–5) and above other facility-based estimates (Table 3). They describe this clinic cohort, as measured, and not the children of Afgooye district.Table 3Present findings compared with published facility-based studies of undernutrition in children under five.Study, settingCountryFacility typeNAge (months)PeriodStuntingWastingPresent study, Afgooye HospitalSomaliaHospital growth monitoring4226–59Feb–Mar 202594.3%79.9%Ali et al. Differences in facility type, referral role, age eligibility, season and methods limit direct comparability.4.2.Reliability of the estimatesBecause the estimates are exceptionally high, measurement and data error must be considered, and we cannot exclude them. No flagged-value screening, duplicate measurement or inter-observer standardization was performed, and Z-score distributions are not available, so we cannot demonstrate that the estimates are free of error. The reported proportions themselves also warrant caution: if Z-scores were approximately normal, 79.9% below −2 and 3.8% below −3 for WHZ imply a mean near −2.3 and an SD of about 0.4, and the HAZ proportions imply a mean near −3.1 and an SD of about 0.7. These are narrower than the spread of about 1 usually seen in survey data, and may indicate measurement or data-handling problems, although a highly selected clinic population could also have a narrower distribution.Two further observations apply. First, wasting by WHZ (79.9%) was twice as frequent as acute malnutrition by MUAC (39.1%). The indicators identify overlapping but non-identical children, so some discordance is expected, but a gap of this size needs reconciliation with repeat measurements, which were not collected. Second, the direction of possible errors matters. An error in length or height shifts HAZ and WHZ in opposite directions, so one systematic length error cannot inflate stunting and wasting together. Underestimated weight (for example from scale zeroing or clothing) would raise wasting but not stunting, and overestimated age would raise stunting but not wasting. Very high prevalence of both therefore implies a genuinely vulnerable group, more than one independent source of error, or a computational or coding problem; the present data cannot distinguish among these.4.3.Comparison with other studiesFacility-based studies share the health-seeking selection of our cohort and are better comparators than population surveys, yet their estimates vary widely (Table 3). Stunting ranged from 14.4% in a Nepalese paediatric outpatient department (13) to 68.2% in the nearby Afgoi preprint (8), and reviews of paediatric hospital populations report undernutrition from 2.5 to 51% depending on population and definitions (14). This heterogeneity reflects referral role, whether a facility runs a nutrition programme that concentrates malnourished children, inclusion of sick or admitted children, underlying community burden, season and methods. Clinic-derived prevalence can diverge substantially from community prevalence and should not be used as a proxy for it (15). Our estimates lie above the range of the comparators in Table 3, including the Afgoi preprint, which was conducted in the same period; the two reports are complementary facility observations rather than independent district estimates.4.4.Possible explanations (hypotheses)The data cannot test the following explanations. Selection: caregivers who attend growth monitoring may do so because of concern about growth or illness, and recruitment from the attendance register would then enrol a more malnourished subgroup. Season: data were collected in the Jilaal dry season, when food and water scarcity and infection risk may be higher (7); we cannot say whether this is a seasonal peak. Displacement: displaced children may be over-represented among attendees and are widely reported to face compounded nutritional risk, but displacement status was not recorded, so this can be neither supported nor excluded. A community-based study of children in IDP camps in Hargeisa, Somaliland, reported 21.1% stunting (16); although design, age range and setting differ, it indicates that displacement does not by itself imply prevalence of the magnitude seen here.4.5.Feeding and morbidityReported prior exclusive breastfeeding (20.6%) is lower than the 33.7% reported for infants under six months in the 2020 national survey (3), but the indicators are not equivalent because ours is a retrospective report across all ages. Low colostrum feeding, incomplete vaccination and frequent recent diarrhoea suggest considerable clinical vulnerability in this cohort. This cross-sectional descriptive study cannot show whether these characteristics are related to stunting or wasting.4.6.Strengths and limitationsStrengths include use of WHO standards and procedures, three complementary anthropometric indicators, confidence intervals, and transparent reporting of data-quality gaps. Limitations are as follows. Recruitment was consecutive and non-probabilistic at a single hospital over two months, which introduces selection bias and prevents generalization, and no screening log exists to characterize non-participants. Duplicate measurements and inter-observer standardization were not performed, so measurement error cannot be excluded. The source of age data, oedema status and enrolment in nutrition programmes were not documented, all of which affect Z-scores and case mix. Feeding and illness data are caregiver-reported and prone to recall bias. Displacement status was not recorded. The design is descriptive, and no analysis of determinants was undertaken.4.7.ImplicationsAt facility level, children identified with growth faltering or acute malnutrition need guideline-based assessment, treatment or referral, feeding counselling, immunization catch-up and evaluation of recurrent infection. These findings should not guide district planning, which needs representative, seasonally repeated surveillance with duplicate measurements, routine recording of displacement status, and samples powered for comparison between host-community and displaced children.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionChildren attending Afgooye Hospital for growth monitoring in February–March 2025 had a very high burden of stunting (94.3%) and wasting (79.9%), with 39.1% acutely malnourished by MUAC, as recorded and not independently verified. These findings describe a single-facility, health-seeking cohort and do not represent Afgooye district. They support strengthened facility-based nutrition care and representative community surveillance across seasons that includes displacement status and quality-controlled anthropometry.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionStunting reflects chronic impairment of linear growth, and wasting reflects recent weight loss relative to length or height. Both increase the risk of illness and death and can impair development and later health (1, 2).Somalia faces recurrent drought, conflict, displacement, food insecurity and limited health and WASH services (3–7). The 2020 Somali Health and Demographic Survey reported stunting in 26.9% and wasting in 11.9% of children under five (3), and the 2019 Somalia Micronutrient Survey reported 17.2% stunting and 11.0% wasting (4, 5). The 2025 IPC analysis described serious acute malnutrition across the country during the Jilaal dry season (7). Population estimates are essential benchmarks, but they do not describe the case mix of children who attend a health facility.Afgooye district, Lower Shabelle, is home to both host-community and internally displaced populations. A recent preprint from two facilities in Afgoi District reported stunting of 68.2% and wasting of 58.3% among 384 children under five (8). Because that study overlaps in place and time with ours, we do not claim novelty on location. Our contribution is a hospital growth-monitoring cohort of children aged 6–59 months in which stunting, wasting and MUAC were assessed together, and in which we explicitly examine the reliability of extreme anthropometric estimates and the limits of what a facility sample can show. The objective was to describe stunting, wasting, MUAC status, and selected socio-demographic, feeding and recent-illness characteristics in this cohort. 2.1.Design and settingWe conducted a facility-based cross-sectional study from February to March 2025 at Afgooye Hospital, about 30 km from Mogadishu, which provides maternal and child health services including growth monitoring. The study characterizes children attending this service; it was not designed to estimate community or district prevalence. 2.2.ParticipantsChildren aged 6–59 months attending the hospital for growth monitoring were eligible, and caregivers gave informed consent. Children already enrolled at an earlier visit were excluded to avoid duplicates. The study records do not specify whether children already enrolled in a nutrition programme, referred for acute malnutrition or admitted as inpatients were eligible, or whether bilateral pitting oedema was assessed; these gaps are acknowledged as limitations. 2.3.Sample size and recruitmentThe single-proportion formula was used with 95% confidence, 5% absolute precision and an expected prevalence of 50% [which maximizes p(1 − p) when no reliable local estimate exists], giving 384 children; adding 10% for non-response gave a target of 422. The calculation addresses precision of a prevalence estimate, not power for association analyses. Eligible children were recruited consecutively from the clinic attendance register until 422 were enrolled. This non-probability approach may over-represent children whose caregivers sought care because of growth or health concerns, limiting generalizability. 2.4.Data collectionTrained data collectors used an interviewer-administered questionnaire covering socio-demographic characteristics, feeding history, recent illness and vaccination, supplemented by review of vaccination cards and medical records. Completed questionnaires were checked daily for completeness and consistency. Food-group questions were not analysed because the questionnaire did not define a reproducible recall period or a validated dietary-diversity score. Displacement status (host community versus internally displaced) was not collected and was not inferred retrospectively; no analysis by displacement status is reported. 2.5.Definitions of variablesDefinitions applied in this analysis were as follows; caregiver report was the source unless stated.Vaccination: complete if the card or caregiver report documented all doses due for the child’s age in the Somali EPI schedule (BCG, OPV0, three doses of OPV and pentavalent, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, and measles-containing vaccine from 9 months); incomplete if at least one but not all due doses were received; none if no dose was documented or reported. Assessment against age-appropriate doses prevented infants under 9 months being classed as incomplete for measles vaccine alone.Colostrum feeding: the first yellowish milk was given rather than discarded. Prior exclusive breastfeeding: only breast milk (apart from oral rehydration salts, vitamins, minerals or prescribed medicines) during the first six months of life; this is a retrospective report for children of all ages and is not equivalent to the survey indicator restricted to infants under six months. Currently breastfeeding: any breast milk at interview.Recent illness (preceding two weeks): diarrhoea was three or more loose or watery stools in 24 h; respiratory-infection symptoms were cough with short, rapid or difficult breathing attributed to a chest problem; fever was caregiver-reported and not measured. History of measles: reported clinical diagnosis at any time or documentation in the record. Deworming: albendazole or mebendazole in the previous six months, by report or record.Caregiver education: no formal education versus any formal schooling. Household income: caregiver-reported total household income in the previous month, in US dollars, categorized as below versus at or above US$100. 2.6.Anthropometric measurement and data qualityMeasurements followed WHO procedures. Weight was measured to the nearest 0.1 kg on a Salter scale with the child in light clothing. Recumbent length was measured for children under 24 months and standing height with a mechanical stadiometer from 24 months. MUAC was measured with a tricolour tape Data collectors were trained, equipment was checked, and forms were reviewed daily. The source used to establish each child’s age (birth certificate, health card or caregiver recall) was not documented. Duplicate measurements and formal inter-observer standardization were not carried out.No flagged-value screening, independent re-entry of data or other formal data-quality audit was performed or documented, and Z-score distributions were not retained for this report. Prevalence estimates are therefore reported as recorded and have not been independently verified; the implications are discussed in Section 4.2. 2.7.Nutritional statusHeight-for-age (HAZ) and weight-for-height (WHZ) Z-scores were calculated with WHO Anthro and the WHO Child Growth Standards. Stunting was HAZ < −2 SD (severe <−3 SD) and wasting was WHZ < −2 SD (severe <−3 SD). By MUAC, <11.5 cm indicated severe and 11.5 to <12.5 cm moderate acute malnutrition. WHZ- and MUAC-based classifications were compared at the aggregate level only. 2.8.Statistical analysisData were analysed in SPSS version 26. We report counts and percentages with Wilson 95% confidence intervals. The study was not designed to identify determinants, and we did not fit regression models for three reasons: (i) only 24 children were not stunted (and 85 not wasted), so models with several covariates would be unstable and prone to sparse-data bias; (ii) the sample size was calculated for prevalence precision rather than for association analyses; and (iii) odds ratios from logistic models overstate prevalence ratios when the outcome is common, and non-random facility selection would make any such estimate hard to interpret. No p-values or adjusted estimates are presented, and statements about associated factors are not made. 2.9.Ethical approvalThe Institutional Review Board of SIMAD University, Mogadishu, approved the study. Written and verbal informed consent was obtained from caregivers. Confidentiality and anonymity were maintained. 3.1.ParticipantsA total of 422 children were analysed. Counts of children screened, ineligible, declining or excluded for incomplete anthropometry were not recorded, so a participant-flow diagram cannot be provided. papers.title_original: Undernutrition among children aged 6–59 months attending Afgooye Hospital, Somalia: a facility-based cross-sectional study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the prevalence of undernutrition among children aged 6–59 months attending Afgooye Hospital, Somalia, to inform public health interventions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A facility-based cross-sectional study was conducted at Afgooye Hospital, Somalia, between February and March 2025, involving 422 children aged 6–59 months.
analysis.methods: The study used a single-proportion formula to calculate the sample size with 95% confidence, 5% absolute precision, and an expected prevalence of 50%. Data were collected via an interviewer-administered questionnaire, and caregiver reports were verified against vaccination cards and medical records.
analysis.main_results: Among the 422 children, 94.3% (95% CI 91.7–96.1) were stunted, 55.9% severely stunted, 79.9% (95% CI 75.8–83.4) were wasted by weight-for-height Z-score, and 39.1% (95% CI 34.6–43.8) had acute malnutrition by MUAC.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest a high prevalence of undernutrition in this clinic cohort, which may indicate measurement or data-handling issues, or a highly selected population with limited variability in nutritional status.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results highlight the urgent need for targeted nutrition interventions in Afgooye Hospital and provide baseline data for future studies on undernutrition in the region.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The non-probability sampling approach may over-represent children with growth or health concerns, limiting generalizability, and the confidence intervals assume independent sampling without accounting for selection bias or measurement error.

analysis.summary_en: This facility-based cross-sectional study conducted at Afgooye Hospital, Somalia, between February and March 2025, assessed undernutrition among 422 children aged 6–59 months. The study found that 94.3% were stunted, 55.9% severely stunted, 79.9% wasted by weight-for-height Z-score, and 39.1% had acute malnutrition by MUAC. These results are based on caregiver-reported data verified against medical records. The study acknowledges limitations, including potential selection bias due to non-probability sampling and the assumption of independent sampling in confidence intervals. The high prevalence of undernutrition underscores the need for targeted interventions in the region, though the findings may not be generalizable beyond the clinic setting.

papers.title: Sarampión: de la eliminación al rebrote. Revisión de la literatura y recomendaciones actuales
papers.abstract: El sarampión es una enfermedad viral altamente contagiosa, prevenible por vacunación y de notificación obligatoria, que representa un problema de salud pública vigente. Su agente causal es el virus del sarampión (familia Paramyxoviridae), de serotipo único, transmitido por vía aérea con un número reproductivo básico de 12 a 18. La presentación clínica clásica incluye un pródromo de fiebre, tos, coriza y conjuntivitis, seguido de las manchas de Koplik y un exantema maculopapular cefalocaudal. El diagnóstico se confirma mediante serología (IgM específica), reacción en cadena de la polimerasa o cultivo viral. El tratamiento es fundamentalmente de soporte; en pacientes pediátricos, la vitamina A reduce la mortalidad hasta un 62%, por lo que está recomendada por la OMS en este grupo de pacientes. Las complicaciones ocurren en aproximadamente el 30% de los casos; las más frecuentes son diarrea (8%) y otitis media (7-9%), y las complicaciones graves incluyen neumonía, diarrea, encefalitis aguda, encefalomielitis aguda posinfecciosa y, a largo plazo, panencefalitis esclerosante subaguda. Las poblaciones más vulnerables son los menores de 5 años, los adultos jóvenes sin inmunización previa, las embarazadas y los inmunocomprometidos. La vacuna triple vírica (sarampión, rubeola y parotiditis) tiene una eficacia del 97% tras dos dosis y requiere una cobertura poblacional superior al 93% para alcanzar la inmunidad de rebaño. En México, la cobertura vacunal ha disminuido significativamente, lo que derivó en más de 12,000 casos confirmados y más de 33 defunciones durante el brote de 2025-2026, afectando mayoritariamente a niños no vacunados. La profilaxis posexposición con la vacuna triple vírica en un plazo de 72 horas, o con inmunoglobulina en un plazo de 6 días, está indicada para personas susceptibles de alto riesgo. La coordinación mundial, las campañas de vacunación sostenidas y una mayor vigilancia clínica siguen siendo fundamentales para frenar la transmisión.

analysis.summary_en: This study addresses the ongoing public health problem of measles, emphasizing its high contagiousness and the importance of vaccination. It outlines the clinical presentation, diagnostic methods, and treatment recommendations, particularly highlighting the role of vitamin A in reducing mortality among pediatric patients. The paper also discusses the impact of declining vaccination coverage, as seen in Mexico during the 2025-2026 outbreak, which resulted in over 12,000 confirmed cases and more than 33 deaths. The findings underscore the necessity of sustained vaccination campaigns and clinical vigilance to control transmission. However, the study does not provide detailed statistical analyses or specific outcomes from interventions, which limits the strength of the evidence. The authors conclude that global coordination and improved surveillance remain critical for preventing measles resurgence.

papers.title_zh: Sarampión: de la eliminación al rebrote.文学修订与实际建议
papers.source_body_en: El sarampión es una enfermedad viral altamente contagiosa, prevenible por vacunación y de notificación obligatoria, que representa un problema de salud pública vigente. Su agente causal es el virus del sarampión (familia Paramyxoviridae), de serotipo único, transmitido por vía aérea con un número reproductivo básico de 12 a 18. La presentación clínica clásica incluye un pródromo de fiebre, tos, coriza y conjuntivitis, seguido de las manchas de Koplik y un exantema maculopapular cefalocaudal. El diagnóstico se confirma mediante serología (IgM específica), reacción en cadena de la polimerasa o cultivo viral. El tratamiento es fundamentalmente de soporte; en pacientes pediátricos, la vitamina A reduce la mortalidad hasta un 62%, por lo que está recomendada por la OMS en este grupo de pacientes. Las complicaciones ocurren en aproximadamente el 30% de los casos; las más frecuentes son diarrea (8%) y otitis media (7-9%), y las complicaciones graves incluyen neumonía, diarrea, encefalitis aguda, encefalomielitis aguda posinfecciosa y, a largo plazo, panencefalitis esclerosante subaguda. Las poblaciones más vulnerables son los menores de 5 años, los adultos jóvenes sin inmunización previa, las embarazadas y los inmunocomprometidos. La vacuna triple vírica (sarampión, rubeola y parotiditis) tiene una eficacia del 97% tras dos dosis y requiere una cobertura poblacional superior al 93% para alcanzar la inmunidad de rebaño. En México, la cobertura vacunal ha disminuido significativamente, lo que derivó en más de 12,000 casos confirmados y más de 33 defunciones durante el brote de 2025-2026, afectando mayoritariamente a niños no vacunados. La profilaxis posexposición con la vacuna triple vírica en un plazo de 72 horas, o con inmunoglobulina en un plazo de 6 días, está indicada para personas susceptibles de alto riesgo. La coordinación mundial, las campañas de vacunación sostenidas y una mayor vigilancia clínica siguen siendo fundamentales para frenar la transmisión.

papers.full_text: AbstractThe evolution of medical epistemology from the unassailable authority of eminence to the empirical rigour of evidence has prepared the healthcare system for its most profound transformation yet, intelligence-based medicine. Driven by the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), this emerging era offers unprecedented capabilities to process complex health data and personalise patient care within high-stakes environments like emergency departments. However, this paradigm shift simultaneously introduces a critical risk of modernised, digital dogma, manifesting as algorithmic paternalism. If AI systems are deployed without rigorous oversight, they threaten to silently amplify historical biases, diagnostic inaccuracies, and outdated clinical heuristics, trading the unquestioned authority of historical figures for the presumed infallibility of machines. To safeguard care in emergency departments, AI must not operate unchecked. Adapting existing Learning Health System frameworks offers a pragmatic solution to govern AI integration. By embedding these computational technologies within continuous, self-correcting clinical ecosystems, departments can enforce robust data hygiene and rigorously audit data provenance. An essential component of this approach is separating objective safety surveillance and adverse event reporting from the algorithm’s internal learning mechanisms to detect epistemic drift and automation bias. Ultimately, the successful and safe integration of intelligence-based medicine depends on an unwavering commitment to transparent governance. When computational power is harnessed as a regulated, transparent tool within an LHS, AI can actively dismantle entrenched clinical dogma, ensuring future care is anchored in dynamic, validated evidence rather than perpetuating the medical errors propagated by eminence from the past.Keywords: artificial intelligence, evidence-based medicine, intelligence-based medicine, learning health systems, medical dogma, medical epistemology 6.ConclusionThe evolution of medical epistemology from the unassailable authority of eminence to the empirical rigour of evidence has prepared the healthcare system for its most profound transformation yet, the dawn of intelligence-based medicine. While AI offers unprecedented capabilities to process complex health data and personalise patient care, it simultaneously introduces the risk of a modernised, digital dogma. If deployed without rigorous oversight, algorithmic systems threaten to silently amplify historical biases, diagnostic inaccuracies, and outdated clinical heuristics. By embedding these technologies within the continuous, self-correcting frameworks of learning health systems, separating performance surveillance from internal model learning, and aggressively auditing data provenance, we can safeguard clinical care in emergency departments. Ultimately, the successful integration of AI depends not just on computational power, but on our unwavering commitment to transparent governance, ensuring these tools actively dismantle entrenched dogma rather than perpetuating the errors of the past. 1.IntroductionMedical epistemology, the philosophical study of how medical knowledge is acquired, validated, and ultimately applied to patient care, has undergone profound transformation throughout human history (1). This evolution of clinical truth can be broadly delineated into three distinct eras (Table 1) (2). For centuries eminence-based medicine governed healthcare through deeply embedded philosophical theory, tradition, and the unquestioned authority of esteemed physicians (3). This foundational period eventually gave way to the era of evidence-based medicine, catalysed by watershed breakthroughs such as the discovery and adoption of germ theory, centring clinical care through the combination of external evidence, individual expertise and patient values and expectations (4). Today, the medical field stands at the precipice of a third revolutionary epoch: intelligence-based medicine. Defined by the deep integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday care, this emerging phase shifts the locus of knowledge from static, population-level evidence to dynamic, hyper-personalised insights (5).Table 1Evolution of medical epistemology.Epistemological eraDimensionEminenceEvidenceIntelligenceIntroductionPrior to late 20th centuryLate 20th century (1990s)Early 21st century (2020s)Epistemic authorityThe Expert: Seniority, clinical intuition, historical precedence, and accumulated personal experience.The Method: Scientific empiricism, rigorous study design and statistical significance.The Algorithm: Pattern recognition, probabilistic modelling, and high-dimensional data analysisSources of knowledgeClinical lore, anecdotes, traditional texts, unstructured and expert opinionRandomised controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical guidelinesRoutinely collected data, peer reviewed, grey, professional and popular literatureStrengths at time of introductionDecisional certainty, standardised training and practisesObjective, reproducible care, patient focused, physician aligned and evaluativePersonalised care, consolidation of vast amounts of informationInherent Limits/FragilityInflexible, dogmatic, non-evaluativePopulation bias, malfeasance, labour intensiveprocess-blind, non-evaluative, automation biasDespite these paradigm shifts in medical epistemology, the underlying threat of medical dogma remains a persistent challenge across all three eras (6, 7). Medical dogma can be defined as the rigid, uncritical acceptance of clinical beliefs or practises, often maintained despite an absence of robust support or in the face of contradictory data (6, 7). This phenomenon defined the era of eminence-based medicine. While evidence-based medicine was designed to dismantle such rigid thinking, dogma continues to be a constant threat in this era. It is frequently driven by the lingering influence of eminence, which has found a powerful new vehicle in social media, where charismatic experts and rapid information sharing can entrench unverified clinical opinions as accepted truths (7, 8). Given the birth of free open access medical education by the critical care specialties, the paucity of high-quality evidence in emergency medicine and the boom of information modalities, emergency departments are particularly vulnerable (9).As we transition toward intelligence-based medicine, the risk of persistent dogmatic practise is not eliminated but potentially amplified. The opacity of AI deeply embedded within information systems can lead to an algorithmic paternalism where clinicians might unknowingly follow the advice of computational outputs, trading the unquestioned authority of historical physicians and medical influencers for the presumed infallibility of machines (10). Optimising intelligence-based medicine therefore requires transparent mechanisms to ensure it functions as an objective tool to detect and disrupt entrenched clinical dogma, rather than a silent amplifier of historical errors. Rather than requiring complete reinvention, existing learning health system frameworks can be refined to act as essential guardrails, subjecting AI inputs to rigorous governance and continuous evaluation. This approach includes systematic assessments of data provenance and real-time surveillance of data accuracy to detect epistemic drift. 2.Eminence based medicineThe epoch of eminence-based medicine represents the longest phase in the history of medical epistemology, spanning roughly from classical antiquity around 400 BCE and persisting well into the late 19th century (2). During these millennia, the foundations of medical practise were constructed not upon empirical observation, but upon sweeping, rigid philosophical frameworks (2, 11). In ancient traditions, most notably the humoral theories championed by Hippocrates, disease was fundamentally rationalised as an imbalance of elemental forces rather than a specific biological pathology (12). These early frameworks relied heavily on deductive reasoning drawn from abstract, untested principles, assuming that human physiology perfectly mirrored the macrocosm of the natural world (12).The intersection of philosophical absolutism and early medical practise cultivated a deeply authoritarian culture within the healing arts (13). Clinical hierarchies were dominated by esteemed figures whose instructions were treated as infallible doctrine (14, 15). In this environment, the hierarchy of knowledge placed the reputation, charisma, and intuition of the doctor far above the reality of the patient experience (16). The culture produced was strictly authoritarian over evidence; questioning a senior physician or challenging an established classical text was viewed as an act of professional rebellion rather than a legitimate scientific inquiry (14). An esteemed physician could rely entirely on personal anecdote and theoretical justification to mandate dangerous treatments such as trepanation, the practise of boring holes into a living patient’s skull to release trapped metaphysical humours, stagnant blood, or evil spirits to cure seizures and mental illness (14).For eminence to remain the absolute standard of truth for centuries was not only a product of professional arrogance, but because the medical community lacked technological infrastructure to support a more evidence-based approach (17, 18). The very concept of systematically evaluating treatments was slow, owing to the lack of digital capabilities (19). In an era where information was recorded manually and shared slowly across vast distances, the ability to coordinate, collect, and mathematically analyse data across multiple centres was impossible (18). 3.Evidence based medicineThe introduction of evidence-based medicine was a profound epistemological shock, demanding that clinical truth no longer be derived from ancient texts or the intuition of a master physician, but from replicable empirical data (18, 19). The breaking point for the centuries long grip of eminence-based medicine arrived not through a philosophical debate but was sparked by the undeniable visualisation of pathology and accompanying germ theory (4, 18). Championed in the 19th century by pioneers like Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch, this paradigm shift demonstrated that specific, observable microorganisms caused specific diseases, completely dismantling the abstract, unprovable tenets of humoral imbalance (12). Acceptance however was bitterly contested and painstakingly slow (1, 2, 4, 15). The early refusal to accept germ theory and empirical clinical data was deeply rooted in the preservation of professional prestige and cognitive dissonance (2). One of the more prominent historical examples was Ignaz Semmelweis who, despite demonstrating that physicians were transmitting fatal puerperal fever to mothers and mandating handwashing, was ostracised and driven out of the profession (20). The medical establishment found it deeply offensive to suggest that a gentleman’s hands could be unclean, allowing their bruised egos and entrenched dogma to completely override clear, statistical evidence of mortality reduction (20). This dogmatic persistence highlighted a critical vulnerability in the evolution of medicine that persists today, that evidence alone is insufficient to create change (6, 7).The eventual embrace of evidence-based medicine required more than just the initial visualisation of pathogens; it necessitated an entire ecosystem of new methodological and technological frameworks made available through the digital era (1, 4, 18, 19). The formalisation of randomised controlled trials, globalised data aggregation, and rapid scientific dissemination eventually catalysed and shaped the widespread acceptance of evidence-based medicine (15, 18, 19).The integrity of evidence-based medicine was not without its challenges, the greatest being scientific malfeasance (21). High-profile fraud such as Andrew Wakefield’s fabricated manuscript linking the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine to autism, and Joachim Boldt’s extensive falsification of hydroxyethyl starch trials, demonstrate how fraudulent research can infiltrate and corrupt clinical guidelines, social expectations and compromise patient safety for decades (22–24). These breaches fundamentally destabilised the epistemic trust required for evidence-based medicine to be embraced and are still so deeply intwined that despite retractions and public discourse, remnants continue to influence care (22, 25).The shadow of eminence-based medicine also continues to linger and actively threaten clinical decision making today, paradoxically fuelled by modern digital technology (26). While evidence-based medicine relies on the slow, methodical accumulation of peer reviewed data, the architecture of social media and digital communication thrives on speed, confidence, and controversy (27, 28). Charismatic experts and social media influencers can now bypass rigorous scientific scrutiny, broadcasting anecdotal successes or theoretical opinions directly to millions of practitioners and patients instantly (27–29). In this digital environment, algorithmic amplification often elevates a compelling narrative over nuanced, statistically sound evidence (30). This creates a dangerous backdoor for eminence to reassert itself, allowing individuals to shape practise patterns based on their digital influence rather than robust clinical validation (30). As we prepare to integrate even more advanced technologies into care, we must recognise that the digital age has not eradicated medical dogma, it has merely provided it with a faster, more pervasive platform (28, 30). 4.Intelligence based medicineThe trajectory toward intelligence-based medicine represents the latest paradigm shift in clinical epistemology (5). Intelligence-based medicine transitions clinical decision making from the static, population-level approach of evidence-based medicine to dynamic computational synthesis by integrating available research, genomics, biometrics, health records, and imaging to deliver hyper-personalised guidance directly at the point of care (31). Following accelerated development of AI in the 1950s, the rapid adoption of intelligence-based care began in the earl 2020s, catalysed by the convergence of computationally affordable deep learning architectures, massive multimodal datasets, and generative AI (5, 31).While frequently conceptualised as a homogeneous entity, artificial intelligence encompasses distinct modalities with unique risk profiles and governance requirements. Rule-based clinical decision support systems execute predetermined logic to guide established protocols. In contrast, prognostic machine learning models dynamically analyse high-dimensional data to forecast outcomes. However, these models are distinctly vulnerable to subtle algorithmic drift, causing accuracy and calibration to degrade over time as patient demographics and clinical practises evolve. Generative artificial intelligence, particularly large language models, offers substantial advantages over simpler computational tools by processing and synthesising unstructured clinical narratives into cohesive insights. Despite this utility, generative models introduce profound epistemic vulnerabilities, notably the generation of factually incorrect outputs and the potentiation of automation bias. This phenomenon risks the erosion of foundational critical thinking, as clinicians facing uncertainty may uncritically defer to the machine, over relying on persuasively worded but potentially flawed computational advice.Unlike the fiercely debated shift to evidence-based medicine, the transition to intelligence-based care is advancing at an unprecedented pace, driven by the pervasive adoption of AI in everyday life (31). Because the integration of AI into clinical workflows brings significant threats alongside its transformative benefits, accelerating this paradigm shift requires robust epistemological guardrails (32). The black box nature of complex machine learning models frequently obscures the underlying logic, making verification extraordinarily difficult for bedside clinicians and patients (32, 33). This opacity risks a perilous regression to eminence-based medicine and emergence of digital dogma, wherein clinicians facing algorithmic uncertainty may uncritically defer to the machine just as classical practitioners once yielded to the unproven pronouncements of esteemed physicians and social media influencers (11, 12, 14, 29, 32). This phenomenon, known as automation bias, risks eroding foundational critical thinking and diagnostic skills, while subtle algorithmic drift can cause model accuracy to quietly degrade over time as patient demographics and clinical practises evolve and new evidence is discovered (31, 32).While artificial intelligence and algorithmic decision-support systems promise unprecedented objectivity, they are trained using highly variable datasets. Umbrella reviews assessing therapeutic interventions in emergency medicine indicate that only a marginal proportion (2.8%) of evaluated meta-analyses meet stringent criteria for high-quality evidence (34). Consequently, clinical practise frequently necessitates reliance on quasi-evidence, observational consensus, or subjective heuristics. The datasets used to train machine learning models are therefore inherently vulnerable to implicit biases, systemic inequities, and eminence-driven practise patterns (32, 33). This creates a profound epistemic risk. While retracted manuscripts exhibit distinct statistical features, they historically bypass human scrutiny to influence subsequent literature. Consequently, the capacity of an algorithm to autonomously detect and filter embedded misinformation represents a substantial functional limitation. When computational power is harnessed as a regulated, transparent tool within an LHS, AI can actively dismantle entrenched clinical dogma, ensuring future care is anchored in dynamic, validated evidence rather than perpetuating the medical errors propagated by eminence from the past.Keywords: artificial intelligence, evidence-based medicine, intelligence-based medicine, learning health systems, medical dogma, medical epistemology
full_text_sections.conclusion: 6.ConclusionThe evolution of medical epistemology from the unassailable authority of eminence to the empirical rigour of evidence has prepared the healthcare system for its most profound transformation yet, the dawn of intelligence-based medicine. While AI offers unprecedented capabilities to process complex health data and personalise patient care, it simultaneously introduces the risk of a modernised, digital dogma. If deployed without rigorous oversight, algorithmic systems threaten to silently amplify historical biases, diagnostic inaccuracies, and outdated clinical heuristics. By embedding these technologies within the continuous, self-correcting frameworks of learning health systems, separating performance surveillance from internal model learning, and aggressively auditing data provenance, we can safeguard clinical care in emergency departments. Ultimately, the successful integration of AI depends not just on computational power, but on our unwavering commitment to transparent governance, ensuring these tools actively dismantle entrenched dogma rather than perpetuating the errors of the past.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionMedical epistemology, the philosophical study of how medical knowledge is acquired, validated, and ultimately applied to patient care, has undergone profound transformation throughout human history (1). This evolution of clinical truth can be broadly delineated into three distinct eras (Table 1) (2). For centuries eminence-based medicine governed healthcare through deeply embedded philosophical theory, tradition, and the unquestioned authority of esteemed physicians (3). This foundational period eventually gave way to the era of evidence-based medicine, catalysed by watershed breakthroughs such as the discovery and adoption of germ theory, centring clinical care through the combination of external evidence, individual expertise and patient values and expectations (4). Today, the medical field stands at the precipice of a third revolutionary epoch: intelligence-based medicine. Defined by the deep integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday care, this emerging phase shifts the locus of knowledge from static, population-level evidence to dynamic, hyper-personalised insights (5).Table 1Evolution of medical epistemology.Epistemological eraDimensionEminenceEvidenceIntelligenceIntroductionPrior to late 20th centuryLate 20th century (1990s)Early 21st century (2020s)Epistemic authorityThe Expert: Seniority, clinical intuition, historical precedence, and accumulated personal experience.The Method: Scientific empiricism, rigorous study design and statistical significance.The Algorithm: Pattern recognition, probabilistic modelling, and high-dimensional data analysisSources of knowledgeClinical lore, anecdotes, traditional texts, unstructured and expert opinionRandomised controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical guidelinesRoutinely collected data, peer reviewed, grey, professional and popular literatureStrengths at time of introductionDecisional certainty, standardised training and practisesObjective, reproducible care, patient focused, physician aligned and evaluativePersonalised care, consolidation of vast amounts of informationInherent Limits/FragilityInflexible, dogmatic, non-evaluativePopulation bias, malfeasance, labour intensiveprocess-blind, non-evaluative, automation biasDespite these paradigm shifts in medical epistemology, the underlying threat of medical dogma remains a persistent challenge across all three eras (6, 7). Medical dogma can be defined as the rigid, uncritical acceptance of clinical beliefs or practises, often maintained despite an absence of robust support or in the face of contradictory data (6, 7). This phenomenon defined the era of eminence-based medicine. While evidence-based medicine was designed to dismantle such rigid thinking, dogma continues to be a constant threat in this era. It is frequently driven by the lingering influence of eminence, which has found a powerful new vehicle in social media, where charismatic experts and rapid information sharing can entrench unverified clinical opinions as accepted truths (7, 8). Given the birth of free open access medical education by the critical care specialties, the paucity of high-quality evidence in emergency medicine and the boom of information modalities, emergency departments are particularly vulnerable (9).As we transition toward intelligence-based medicine, the risk of persistent dogmatic practise is not eliminated but potentially amplified. The opacity of AI deeply embedded within information systems can lead to an algorithmic paternalism where clinicians might unknowingly follow the advice of computational outputs, trading the unquestioned authority of historical physicians and medical influencers for the presumed infallibility of machines (10). Optimising intelligence-based medicine therefore requires transparent mechanisms to ensure it functions as an objective tool to detect and disrupt entrenched clinical dogma, rather than a silent amplifier of historical errors. Rather than requiring complete reinvention, existing learning health system frameworks can be refined to act as essential guardrails, subjecting AI inputs to rigorous governance and continuous evaluation. This approach includes systematic assessments of data provenance and real-time surveillance of data accuracy to detect epistemic drift. 2.Eminence based medicineThe epoch of eminence-based medicine represents the longest phase in the history of medical epistemology, spanning roughly from classical antiquity around 400 BCE and persisting well into the late 19th century (2). During these millennia, the foundations of medical practise were constructed not upon empirical observation, but upon sweeping, rigid philosophical frameworks (2, 11). In ancient traditions, most notably the humoral theories championed by Hippocrates, disease was fundamentally rationalised as an imbalance of elemental forces rather than a specific biological pathology (12). These early frameworks relied heavily on deductive reasoning drawn from abstract, untested principles, assuming that human physiology perfectly mirrored the macrocosm of the natural world (12).The intersection of philosophical absolutism and early medical practise cultivated a deeply authoritarian culture within the healing arts (13). Clinical hierarchies were dominated by esteemed figures whose instructions were treated as infallible doctrine (14, 15). In this environment, the hierarchy of knowledge placed the reputation, charisma, and intuition of the doctor far above the reality of the patient experience (16). The culture produced was strictly authoritarian over evidence; questioning a senior physician or challenging an established classical text was viewed as an act of professional rebellion rather than a legitimate scientific inquiry (14). An esteemed physician could rely entirely on personal anecdote and theoretical justification to mandate dangerous treatments such as trepanation, the practise of boring holes into a living patient’s skull to release trapped metaphysical humours, stagnant blood, or evil spirits to cure seizures and mental illness (14).For eminence to remain the absolute standard of truth for centuries was not only a product of professional arrogance, but because the medical community lacked technological infrastructure to support a more evidence-based approach (17, 18). The very concept of systematically evaluating treatments was slow, owing to the lack of digital capabilities (19). In an era where information was recorded manually and shared slowly across vast distances, the ability to coordinate, collect, and mathematically analyse data across multiple centres was impossible (18). 3.Evidence based medicineThe introduction of evidence-based medicine was a profound epistemological shock, demanding that clinical truth no longer be derived from ancient texts or the intuition of a master physician, but from replicable empirical data (18, 19). The breaking point for the centuries long grip of eminence-based medicine arrived not through a philosophical debate but was sparked by the undeniable visualisation of pathology and accompanying germ theory (4, 18). Championed in the 19th century by pioneers like Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch, this paradigm shift demonstrated that specific, observable microorganisms caused specific diseases, completely dismantling the abstract, unprovable tenets of humoral imbalance (12). Acceptance however was bitterly contested and painstakingly slow (1, 2, 4, 15). The early refusal to accept germ theory and empirical clinical data was deeply rooted in the preservation of professional prestige and cognitive dissonance (2). One of the more prominent historical examples was Ignaz Semmelweis who, despite demonstrating that physicians were transmitting fatal puerperal fever to mothers and mandating handwashing, was ostracised and driven out of the profession (20). papers.title_original: From eminence to evidence to intelligence-based medicine: optimising artificial intelligence to disrupt dogma in emergency departments

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the risk of modernised, digital dogma in the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into emergency departments, highlighting the need to prevent algorithmic biases and ensure clinical care remains grounded in validated evidence.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study examined the evolution of medical epistemology and the challenges of integrating AI into clinical practice, focusing on emergency departments and the broader healthcare system.
analysis.methods: The study utilised historical and contemporary examples to evaluate the risks of AI deployment, including the black box nature of machine learning models and the potential for automation bias and epistemic drift.
analysis.main_results: The findings indicate that only a marginal proportion (2.8%) of evaluated meta-analyses in emergency medicine meet stringent criteria for high-quality evidence, and that AI systems are vulnerable to implicit biases and outdated clinical heuristics.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the integration of AI into emergency departments must be governed by transparent frameworks to prevent the emergence of digital dogma, offering a novel approach to align computational power with dynamic, validated evidence.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings inform the need for rigorous oversight and governance of AI systems in emergency medicine to ensure they do not perpetuate historical biases or errors, thereby safeguarding patient care and clinical decision-making.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on historical and general observations rather than specific, target-focused evidence, which limits the strength of its conclusions and necessitates further targeted research.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into emergency departments, highlighting the risks of modernised, digital dogma. It argues that AI systems, if not rigorously overseen, may amplify historical biases and diagnostic inaccuracies, undermining the principles of evidence-based medicine. The authors propose embedding AI within learning health systems to ensure transparency, continuous auditing, and separation of performance surveillance from model learning. They note that only a marginal proportion (2.8%) of evaluated meta-analyses in emergency medicine meet high-quality criteria, underscoring the need for careful governance. The study suggests that AI can actively dismantle entrenched clinical dogma if properly regulated, but its success depends on transparent frameworks that prevent algorithmic drift and automation bias. While the study provides a conceptual framework, it lacks specific, target-focused evidence, limiting its conclusions.

elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,人工智能与急诊部门的整合必须受到透明框架的约束,以防止数字教条的出现,从而提供一种将计算能力与动态、经过验证的证据结合起来的新颖方法。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明需要对急诊医学中的人工智能系统进行严格的监督和治理,以确保它们不会延续历史偏见或错误,从而保障患者护理和临床决策。

Operational Technology Is a Possible Cyberattack Target Operational technology — which consists of network-connected devices that control physical systems like elevators and security systems — is often vulnerable to cyberattacks. Scott Gee, AHA deputy national advisor for cybersecurity and risk, explains why hospital leaders often fail to recognize how ubiquitous OT is in their own facilities, why OT is so vulnerable to attack, and the biggest challenge to protecting OT from cyberattacks and what to do about it. Read the Cyber & Risk Intel Blog AHA Launches New AI Policy and Advocacy Webpage The AHA launched a new webpage, Artificial Intelligence Policy and Advocacy, featuring AHA policy letters, statements, fact sheets, news and other resources. The page also includes stories from hospitals and health systems that have leveraged AI to improve efficiency, support the workforce and enhance patient care. View the AI Policy Webpage Chair File: Hospital Teams Are Ready for Any Emergency Hospitals and health systems train year-round for situations we all hope don’t happen but know far too well do. Hurricanes, tornadoes, wildfires, mass casualty events and other public health emergencies require hospitals to respond quickly, coordinate across multiple organizations and continue caring for patients under incredibly challenging circumstances. Application Deadline: March 31, 2027 Explore the Fellowship A Special Message from Steve Walsh: Looking Ahead Together The American Hospital Association's new president and CEO, Steve Walsh, shares an introductory message with members on his hopes for the future of our nation’s healthcare system and how hospitals and health systems can navigate the generational challenges they face. Read the Special Bulletin Carolyn Boone Lewis Award for Improving Health Outcomes This AHA award recognizes excellence in applying data-informed strategies to effectively improve health outcomes for all. One winner and two finalists will be recognized at the AHA Leadership Summit 2027 in San Diego, July 18-20. Applications are due Dec. 4. Apply for Award Real Affordability Solutions from the Front Lines of Caring The AHA today released a new report highlighting actionable and achievable strategies and solutions to make health care more affordable. Read the Press Release Hope. Healing. Health. Watch AHA's new ad highlighting how hospitals and health systems provide hope, healing and health to the patients and communities they serve.
