news.content_title: Pennsylvania measles cases reach 1,679 across 46 counties as state adds 41 new infections
news.content: Pennsylvania measles cases reach 1,679 across 46 counties as state adds 41 new infections The Brief - Pennsylvania health officials reported 41 new measles cases since Nov. 23, pushing the statewide total to 1,679 across 46 counties in 2026. - The outbreak has resulted in 340 hospitalizations and nine confirmed measles-associated deaths so far this year. - Health officials say fewer than 1% of cases occurred in vaccinated residents and continue urging Pennsylvanians to get the two-dose MMR vaccine. PENNSYLVANIA - Pennsylvania health officials announced Wednesday that the state's ongoing measles outbreak has climbed to 1,679 confirmed cases across 46 counties, with 41 new infections reported since Monday. According to the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH), the outbreak—which began in late April—has led to 340 hospitalizations and nine confirmed measles-associated deaths so far in 2026. Local perspective State health data shows that nearly all infections have occurred in unvaccinated residents, with only five cases—less than 1% of the total—reported among vaccinated individuals. Since the outbreak started, roughly 300 DOH staff members have worked with local communities and health providers to expand access to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine: State nurses have administered more than 12,000 MMR doses in 2026, including nearly 7,600 shots across 292 pop-up vaccination clinics. Statewide vaccine demand has surged well above the typical monthly average of 25,000 doses, with providers administering more than 56,000 doses in September, over 62,000 in October and more than 40,000 so far in November. DOH's response team meets every other week with Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) staff to review cases and coordinate containment efforts. Vaccination guidance By the numbers Health officials emphasize that two doses of the MMR vaccine provide 97% lifetime protection against the virus. Because of ongoing community spread, DOH recommends: - Infants 6 to 11 months old: An early "zero dose" for babies living in or traveling to counties flagged on the state's measles dashboard for sustained transmission. This early shot does not replace the two routine doses. - Children 12 months and older: One dose immediately if unvaccinated, followed by a second dose at least 28 days later. - Adults: Anyone with two documented doses does not need another shot, while adults with only one dose or missing records should consult a health care provider or pharmacist. MMR vaccines are available through primary care providers, county or municipal health departments, DOH State Health Centers, Federally Qualified Health Centers and the Vaccines for Children program. Symptoms and how it spreads What's next Measles is a highly contagious respiratory virus that spreads through breathing, coughing or sneezing, and can linger in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Nearly 20% of Pennsylvanians diagnosed during the outbreak have required hospitalization, and severe complications can include pneumonia and brain swelling. Symptoms typically appear 7 to 21 days after exposure—and people are contagious from four days before until four days after a rash develops. Early signs include: - Fever, cough and runny nose - Red, watery eyes - A rash that starts on the head and spreads downward a few days later Anyone who believes they were exposed and is experiencing symptoms should contact their health care provider or call the state's toll-free hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258). The Source This article was written using a press release from the Pennsylvania Department of Health

news.source_body_en: Pennsylvania measles cases reach 1,679 across 46 counties as state adds 41 new infections The Brief - Pennsylvania health officials reported 41 new measles cases since Nov. 23, pushing the statewide total to 1,679 across 46 counties in 2026. - The outbreak has resulted in 340 hospitalizations and nine confirmed measles-associated deaths so far this year. - Health officials say fewer than 1% of cases occurred in vaccinated residents and continue urging Pennsylvanians to get the two-dose MMR vaccine. PENNSYLVANIA - Pennsylvania health officials announced Wednesday that the state's ongoing measles outbreak has climbed to 1,679 confirmed cases across 46 counties, with 41 new infections reported since Monday. According to the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH), the outbreak—which began in late April—has led to 340 hospitalizations and nine confirmed measles-associated deaths so far in 2026. Local perspective State health data shows that nearly all infections have occurred in unvaccinated residents, with only five cases—less than 1% of the total—reported among vaccinated individuals.

news.rss_summary_html: Measles cases fall in Almaty region following immunization campaign  Qazinform

news.content_title: Measles cases fall in Almaty region following immunization campaign
news.content: Kazinform Kazakhstan Regions Society Law and Order Culture Sport President Politics President Government Parliament International Relations Economy Analytics World Central Asia Eurasia Middle East America Africa EN KZ QZ РУ EN 中文 ЎЗ ق ز kz qz ру en 中文 ўз ق ز Kazakhstan Regions Society Law and Order Culture Sport President Politics President Government Parliament International Relations Economy Analytics World Central Asia Eurasia Middle East America Africa Measles cases fall in Almaty region following immunization campaign 07:09, 25 November 2026 Measles ncidence in Almaty region decreased by 7.2 times thanks to an additional immunization campaign, although children under the age of five still account for the majority of infections, a Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports. Photo credit: Gov.kz Deputy head of the regional aanitary and epidemiological control department Saulet Kapsalamova said, 5,271 measles cases were recorded in the region in 2023-2024, compared with 727 cases in 2025-2026. Health officials attribute the decline to an additional vaccination campaign that immunized 118,000 people during 2024-2025. Data from sanitary authorities show that 74% of measles patients are children under five years old, while 73% of those infected had not been vaccinated. Among the unvaccinated, 30% were below the eligible vaccination age, 32% had medical exemptions, and 38% were unvaccinated due to parental refusal. Measles is a highly contagious viral infection transmitted through airborne droplets. Among people without immunity, one infected person can spread the virus to up to 18 others. Patients can transmit the disease for up to four days before the characteristic rash appears. Health experts say herd immunity must remain above 95% to prevent outbreaks. “Measles should not be regarded as a mild disease. It can cause serious complications such as pneumonia, ear infections and encephalitis. The infection is particularly dangerous for young children,” Kapsalamova said. She also warned about subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare but severe complication that can develop years after a measles infection and lead to progressive brain damage. Effective treatment for a complete cure is still unavailable. According to specialists, vaccination remains the most effective protection against measles. Under Kazakhstan’s national immunization schedule, the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is administered at 12 months and again at six years of age. Two doses provide protective immunity in approximately 97-99% of people. Unvaccinated individuals who have been in contact with infected patients are advised to receive emergency vaccination within 72 hours of exposure. This year, 70% of the 16,947 children scheduled for vaccination in Almaty region have received their shots. In addition, 650 healthcare workers were vaccinated, while 3,212 people under 18 received catch-up immunizations. To monitor the epidemiological situation in schools and other organized groups, authorities conducted 101 inspections and imposed 37 administrative measures. The region has also approved a comprehensive 2026-2027 plan aimed at increasing vaccination coverage. Health officials are monitoring immunization rates, reviewing the validity of medical exemptions and conducting outreach campaigns among citizens who refuse vaccination. Earlier, a one-year-old girl died from measles complications in Atyrau region. Health authorities have also reported a sharp rise in measles cases in West Kazakhstan, while the World Health Organization warned this summer about the risk of new outbreaks due to insufficient childhood vaccination coverage. It should be noted, childhood measles vaccination rates have declined globally since the COVID-19 pandemic, contributing to a sharp resurgence of one of the world's most contagious diseases. news.content_title: Virginia Reported Its First Measles Death in 48 Years. Should You Be Concerned?
news.content: The Virginia Department of Health last week announced the state’s first measles death in 48 years — a child under the age of 4. And the nation has lost the measles-elimination status that it gained in 2000, as cases continue to grow nationwide. Virginia had four measles cases in 2025 , according to the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota. So far this year, the number is 220. VDH says the vast majority of new cases are homegrown and not related to international travel. And that all new cases since October 17 of this year have been in people who were not vaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. Nicole Dickinson RN, director of the emergency department at Sentara Northern Virginia, says they haven’t seen a significant uptick in measles cases. And that people should hold tight to the preventative procedures they’ve already taken. If you have any symptoms of the measles, she says, follow up with your primary care professional. And she repeated the most important advice for dealing with almost any communicable disease: “If you’re sick, stay home.” Here’s what Dr. Sujata Ambardar , an infectious disease physician at Inova Fairfax Hospital, wants people in Northern Virginia to know: What Causes Measles Outbreaks? The most obvious explanation for the outbreaks across the country is growing resistance to vaccines. Naturally, a vaccination is Ambardar’s first suggestion for how people should protect themselves. She adds that measles is more contagious than most other airborne infections. “If you have one person with measles in a room, 90 percent of people will get exposed to measles,” she says. That’s much higher than, for example, tuberculosis. That means a mask isn’t going to help much against the measles, she adds. A rash, fever, and/or a cough can be the early symptoms of measles . Rhinitis (nasal congestion and itching) and conjunctivitis can also be signs of the disease. “If there is anybody that has symptoms that you see, then you need to be extremely cautious and would try to obviously not be near them,” Ambardar says. Fortunately, in this area most jurisdictions have “historically been very good about mandating vaccines,” Ambardar says. “And in fact, most colleges won’t let you attend unless you’ve been vaccinated for certain things like measles, mumps, rubella, tetanus, Tdap, and even some of the meningococcal vaccines.” Dickinson advises consulting with your doctor. “Comorbidities do play a role, and people should follow up with practitioners who know them,” she says Do I Need a Booster? Probably not, Ambardar says. She has heard the reports that some people who got vaccinated between 1957 and 1968 “may have gotten vaccines that were inactivated — not a live vaccine — so those people may not have as much of a robust response.” That doesn’t mean you should go running out for a booster, she says. If you’re truly concerned about your protection against measles infection, she recommends getting a titer test. A titer is a blood test that will show whether you have immunity, either through vaccination or by previously having had the disease. “I actually keep [mine] in my desk,” Ambardar says, “because it’s positive, so I never have to get tested again. I would never need a booster.” The bar may be higher for health care workers, she says. They should get their titers checked to be sure. But for the general population, if you’ve been safe, you still should be. “Only if the blood test is negative would I get a booster,” Ambardar says. “Not because it’s an unsafe vaccine, but why get a vaccine if you don’t need it?” “The only time they recommend a booster, they’re saying, is if there’s an outbreak ongoing,” Ambaradar says. If you have incomplete protection and an outbreak is raging, they won’t want to wait until everyone’s titers come back from the lab. “But we’re not in that situation here in the DMV, so I think it’s better just to get a titer if there’s any concern.” Get can’t-miss updates delivered directly to your inbox with our NoVA Daily newsletter

news.content_title: Vaccine gaps fuelling global measles resurgence, WHO warns
news.content: Poor vaccination coverage is fuelling a resurgence in measles outbreaks globally, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned. Although measles deaths are at a record low, 29 million children were left unvaccinated or under-vaccinated in 2025, according to the UN health body's annual assessment of global progress towards eliminating measles, released on Friday. Earlier this month, the United States, Mexico and Bolivia lost their measles elimination status , after the Pan American Health Organization, the WHO's regional agency for the Americas, found the virus had been circulating continuously in each country for at least 12 months. The UK lost its status in January . "Elimination is not the finish line," Dr Kate O'Brien, the WHO's director of immunisation, told reporters at a press briefing to mark the launch of the report on Wednesday. "The recent setbacks we've seen are not a failure of the measles vaccine; they're a failure to reach every child with the vaccine". Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to humans and requires 95 per cent of the community to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks. Children under-five, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems are at greatest risk. According to the WHO, it can cause pneumonia, brain infection, deafness and blindness, death and "immune amnesia", where the virus can weaken the immune system for months or even years. The measles vaccine, which used a weakened (live attenuated) virus in two doses, is safe and highly effective. Dr O'Brien said: "Some of the more recent graduates have never seen a case of measles, but it is back". Diana Chang Blanc, unit head of the essential programme on immunisation at the WHO, said the spread of cases across income levels showed that even in places with strong health systems, small drops in coverage can leave pockets of unvaccinated people that can spread risks far beyond those areas. In 2025, 59 countries had "large or disruptive outbreaks", defined as more than 20 cases per million people over 12 months. Of them, 11 were previously declared measles-free. The US was not among them, as its outbreaks didn't reach the threshold. "It can take years to regain elimination status, whereas it takes only a 12-month period to lose elimination status," said Dr O'Brien. "These are hard-fought gains that countries have made, and protecting them now is more important than ever". Outbreaks were also not confined to poorer nations: 18 were in low-income countries, 34 in middle-income countries and seven in high-income countries. news.content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Boats Grocery Shopping Holidays OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services HEALTH World Health Organization Add Topic New Ohio measles cases this week nearly match total from 2025 Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Nov. 27, 2026, 10:47 a.m. ET Hear this story Ohio is experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with 400 cases reported in 30 counties so far this year. The majority of measles cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, as vaccination rates have fallen below the herd immunity threshold. Nationally, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, causing the U.S. to lose the measles elimination status it had held since 2000. Ohio's measles case count so far in 2026 is nearly three times greater than the numbers from the previous four years combined. On the heels of one person potentially spreading measles across five locations in Western Ohio, which happened roughly a week after a similar situation in Geauga and Lake counties, two more counties joined the list of confirmed cases as the state's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues. ODH is reporting 400 cases in 30 of 88 Ohio counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Nov. 26. That number is nearly eight times (788%) more than the 45 cases reported in all of 2025. Ohio added 42 new cases in the past week, a 35% increase from the 31 new cases reported the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. Coshocton and Monroe counties joined the list this week with three cases total. Ashland, Medina and Wayne counties had the most new cases. Nationally, the United States has officially lost its measles-free status. The disease had been declared eradicated from the US in 2000 in what the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention called a "historic" accomplishment. Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high. As of Nov. 24, Johns Hopkins University counted 6,369 measles cases in the U.S. in 2026, and as of Nov. 25, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 6,038 confirmed measles cases in 47 states plus Washington, D.C. – more than double last year's total of 2,289, USA TODAY reports. That's the highest annual total since 1991. The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles growing in Ohio. These counties report cases in 2026 Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashland: 13 (five new cases) Ashtabula: 58 Coshocton: 2 (first time on list) Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 8 Gallia: 7 (four new cases) Geauga: 69 (four new cases) Hancock: 1 Harrison: 18 Holmes: 15 (one new case) Jackson: 1 Knox: 5 Mahoning: 2 Medina: 40 (12 new cases) Meigs: 4 Mercer: 8 (four new cases) Monroe: 1 (first time on list) Morgan: 3 Morrow: 13 Ottawa: 1 Paulding: 1 Pike: 27 (one new case) Portage: 1 Stark: 1 Trumbull: 19 (three new cases) Tuscarawas: 15 Van Wert: 3 Vinton: 1 Wayne: 59 (five new cases) Wood: 1 The case count for the year reflects previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. When including the 90 measles cases in 2022, Ohio's total so far in 2026 is nearly three times greater than the previous four years combined. Weekly Ohio measles cases by the numbers Total cases in Ohio this year have continued climbing, as reported by ODH: 358 cases in 28 counties on Nov. 19 327 cases in 26 counties on Nov. 12 310 cases in 25 counties on Nov. 5 296 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 29 260 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 22 252 cases in 23 counties on Oct. 15 228 cases in 21 counties on Oct. 8 206 cases in 20 counties on Oct. 1 196 cases in 16 counties on Sept. 24 180 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 17 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6 Measles kills at least nine in Pennsylvania; infant dies of measles in Wisconsin Pennsylvania confirmed its seventh measles-related death of the year on Nov. 16, while New York announced its first measles death in 30 years on Nov. 2, according to USA TODAY. As of Nov. 25, the CDC reports nine measles deaths in the U.S. in 2026. Wisconsin also reported a grim milestone on Nov. 5, with health officials saying that its first measles death since 1990 was that of an infant. Reuters on Nov. 25 reports 14 measles deaths in the U.S. this year: Nine deaths in Pennsylvania, three in Wisconsin, and one each in New York and Virginia. Measles cases on the rise as Ohio vaccination rates fluctuate in state, U.S. Vaccination rates for measles have declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Ohio's vaccination rate for the 2025-26 school year slipped well below the herd immunity threshold, making it susceptible to outbreaks. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of a 2025 Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States, country loses 'eliminated' status The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. The United States has officially lost its measles-free status three decades after the "historic public health achievement" that eliminated the highly infectious disease from the country, the Pan American Health Organization, the part of the World Health Organization that tracks infectious disease in the Americas, announced Nov. 17. Defined by the WHO as freedom from the continuous spread of a disease for at least 12 months, the United States achieved measles elimination status in 2000 in what the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention called a "historic" accomplishment. Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, pointed to gaps in vaccination coverage as a significant culprit. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but they can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before through four days after a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Featured Weekly Ad

The event date is not explicitly stated, but the report was published on 2026-11-27.

The report does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers, but it highlights the risk of measles resurgence in these countries.

news.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Thanksgiving storm World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds CBS Evening News | Full Episodes On the Road Great Question Podcast About Tony Dokoupil Watch CBS News CBS Evening News 9th measles death recorded in Pennsylvania as outbreak surpasses 1,600 cases in the state By Lilia Luciano Lilia Luciano Anchor and Correspondent, "CBS News 24/7" Lilia Luciano is an award-winning journalist and CBS News 24/7 anchor and correspondent based in New York City. Luciano is the recipient of multiple journalism awards, including a Walter Cronkite Award, a regional Edward R. Murrow Award and five regional Emmys. Read Full Bio Lilia Luciano November 23, 2026 / 8:26 PM EST / CBS News Add CBS News on Google Pennsylvania on Monday announced its ninth measles-related death this year as cases continue to surge across the U.S., reaching their highest mark in decades. The death was reported in Centre County, in the middle of the state. The Pennsylvania Department of Health did not provide any further information about the patient. The announcement came just three days after Virginia reported that a child under the age of 5 had died after testing positive for measles. It was Virginia's first measles-related death this year, the state's Health Department said. Pennsylvania's outbreak is the largest in the country, with over 1,600 cases reported, according to the state Department of Health, and the deaths this year are the Keystone State's first from measles in 35 years. In Lancaster County, one woman told CBS News her three children all have measles. The U.S. had eliminated measles by the year 2000, but last week the country lost that status. A country is considered to have eliminated measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data show that about a quarter of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025, when the U.S. saw a 30-year high of 2,289 cases, and that the virus continued to spread. As of last week, there have been 5,838 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. this year, according to the CDC. Dr. Evan Shirey, an infectious disease specialist, said he went from seeing no measles cases to dealing with them "almost every day." 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE He blames misinformation for vaccine hesitancy. "The manifestations of that can just be horrible to see," he said. "Children gasping for air. Seeing a child who is altered, confused, unable to recognize their own mom." Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has long been criticized for casting doubt on vaccine safety, said in the wake of the U.S. losing its measles elimination status, "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles." Kindergarten vaccination rates have fallen below the 95% needed to protect the immunocompromised and infants too young to be vaccinated. Among the latter group: Shirey's 3-month-old son. "I'm absolutely counting down the days," he told CBS News. "I'll have him in there on the date to make sure that I'm doing what I can for him to protect him." The first dose of the MMR vaccine is usually given at 12 to 15 months of age, but can be given as early as 6 months in high-risk cases, such as during an ongoing outbreak. Kerry Breen and Grace Manthey contributed to this report. news.source_body_en: Pennsylvania has recorded its ninth measles-related death of the year, as the state's outbreak surpasses 1,600 cases, marking the highest number in decades. The death was reported in Centre County, and the state's Department of Health noted that this is the first measles-related death in Pennsylvania in 35 years. The U.S. measles cases have surged to 5,838 confirmed cases as of last week, according to the CDC. The outbreak is attributed to a 30-year high in cases from 2025, and experts are highlighting the spread of the virus and the risk to vulnerable populations, including immunocompromised individuals and infants too young to be vaccinated. Evan Shirey, an infectious disease specialist, expressed concern over vaccine hesitancy, citing misinformation as a contributing factor. The state's health officials have not provided further details about the deceased patient, but they emphasize the importance of vaccination to prevent the disease. The outbreak underscores the challenges in maintaining measles elimination status, which the U.S. lost last week.

news.content: U.S. News Politics AI Politics Tech Fact Check Sports Global Iran War Russia-Ukraine Middle East China And Asia Live Blog Better Planet All World News Lifestyle Family & Parenting Entertainment Travel Pets Automotive Relationships Science Health Personal Finance Better Workplaces Readers Choice Opinion My Turn All Opinion Rankings Health Finance Products Education Workplaces Corporate Responsibility All Rankings Watch The 1600 The Royal Report Unconventional From The Paddock Newsmakers Extra Newsletters Dare to Dream Events Essays Podcasts Vantage Insights Magazine CEO Circle Announcements Leadership Dev Pragad Subscribe Sign In U.S. NewsPoliticsAI PoliticsTechFact CheckSports Global Iran WarRussia-UkraineMiddle EastChina And AsiaLive BlogBetter PlanetAll World News Lifestyle Family & ParentingEntertainmentTravelPetsAutomotiveRelationshipsScienceHealthPersonal FinanceBetter WorkplacesReaders Choice Opinion My TurnAll Opinion Rankings HealthCorporate ResponsibilityFinanceProductsEducationWorkAll Rankings Watch The 1600The Royal ReportUnconventionalFrom The PaddockNewsmakers Social FacebookInstagramYouTubeRedditTikTokTwitter/X Extra NewslettersDare to DreamEventsEssaysPodcastsVantageInsightsMagazineCEO CircleAnnouncementsLeadershipDev Pragad Health experts are warning of a potential measles outbreak as millions of Americans travel home for Thanksgiving. The U.S. lost its measles-free status last week after 26 years, with 5,838 cases reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as of November 19 - already double the number in 2025. Ten patients subsequently died, at least five of whom were children, marking the deadliest year since 1991 as the highly contagious virus spreads mainly through the unvaccinated. Measles spreads through the air, and a single infected person can spread the virus to as many as 18 people, making crowded airports and holiday celebrations high-risk areas of exposure. Symptoms typically develop about two weeks after exposure and begin with a high fever followed by a rash that starts on the face and neck. Other signs include fatigue, nasal congestion, and pink eye, and serious complications could lead to blindness and swelling of the brain. The virus currently exists in pockets of the country, but Thanksgiving travel and large family gatherings present a chance for it to spread. Thanksgiving Travel Advice Dr. Alexis Jesup, a family physician with Roper St. Francis Healthcare, recommended wearing a mask while traveling in crowded spaces or around people who are sick, and to stay home if you feel ill. She said: "If you’re not feeling good, stay home. Do a FaceTime, do a video chat with your family to celebrate, and see your doctor if you’re not feeling well." Dr. Kanai Kim, an infectious disease specialist with USF and Tampa General Hospital, added that families should be mindful of where they are traveling, whether it's experiencing an outbreak, and who they are gathering with. She told Fox 13: "Most people haven't seen a case of measles. So they don't understand how bad measles can be... If you've got a vulnerable person like your baby, it's so hard to protect them. It just sweeps through the community." Dr. Kim said parents traveling with their children to areas experiencing measles outbreaks should consult their pediatricians, as an early dose of the vaccine may be appropriate for babies between six and 11 months. Importance of Vaccines In the last two years, over 7,000 measles cases and 13 deaths have been reported - nearly all of whom were either unvaccinated or didn't report whether they were vaccinated. More than 10 percent of cases resulted in hospitalization. Two doses of the 97 percent effective measles mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine usually protect people for life, as does having previously had the disease. Unvaccinated children also risk contracting subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a condition caused by the measles virus destroying brain cells that can start years after an infection but cannot be triggered by the vaccine. It can change a child's personality and cause seizures of involuntary movements, which lead to dementia and problems eating and breathing. It is almost always fatal, but the best way to prevent it is with the measles vaccine. Dr. Jesup said: "Vaccines are available to adults, adolescents, all people at any point in time... If you’re not vaccinated and you have the opportunity, get it." The Americas became the first region in the world to be free of measles in 2016 following a hugely successful vaccination campaign that health officials estimate prevented 6.2 million deaths between 2000 and 2023. Health experts are warning of a potential measles outbreak as millions of Americans travel home for Thanksgiving. The U.S. lost its measles-free status last week after 26 years, with 5,838 cases reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as of November 19 - already double the number in 2025. Ten patients subsequently died, at least five of whom were children, marking the deadliest year since 1991 as the highly contagious virus spreads mainly through the unvaccinated. Read More on News Measles spreads through the air, and a single infected person can spread the virus to as many as 18 people, making crowded airports and holiday celebrations high-risk areas of exposure. Symptoms typically develop about two weeks after exposure and begin with a high fever followed by a rash that starts on the face and neck. Other signs include fatigue, nasal congestion, and pink eye, and serious complications could lead to blindness and swelling of the brain. The virus currently exists in pockets of the country, but Thanksgiving travel and large family gatherings present a chance for it to spread. People move through the Moynihan Train Hall in Manhattan on November 26, 2025, in New York City. | Spencer Platt/Getty Images Thanksgiving Travel Advice Dr. Alexis Jesup, a family physician with Roper St. Francis Healthcare, recommended wearing a mask while traveling in crowded spaces or around people who are sick, and to stay home if you feel ill. Sign up Sign up to Breaking News alerts By clicking “sign up” you are agreeing to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy She said: "If you’re not feeling good, stay home. Do a FaceTime, do a video chat with your family to celebrate, and see your doctor if you’re not feeling well." Dr. Kanai Kim, an infectious disease specialist with USF and Tampa General Hospital, added that families should be mindful of where they are traveling, whether it's experiencing an outbreak, and who they are gathering with. She told Fox 13: "Most people haven't seen a case of measles. So they don't understand how bad measles can be... If you've got a vulnerable person like your baby, it's so hard to protect them. It just sweeps through the community." Dr. Kim said parents traveling with their children to areas experiencing measles outbreaks should consult their pediatricians, as an early dose of the vaccine may be appropriate for babies between six and 11 months. Measles viral disease, human skin covered with measles rash. | Getty Images Importance of Vaccines In the last two years, over 7,000 measles cases and 13 deaths have been reported - nearly all of whom were either unvaccinated or didn't report whether they were vaccinated. More than 10 percent of cases resulted in hospitalization. Two doses of the 97 percent effective measles mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine usually protect people for life, as does having previously had the disease. Unvaccinated children also risk contracting subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a condition caused by the measles virus destroying brain cells that can start years after an infection but cannot be triggered by the vaccine. It can change a child's personality and cause seizures of involuntary movements, which lead to dementia and problems eating and breathing. It is almost always fatal, but the best way to prevent it is with the measles vaccine. Dr. Jesup said: "Vaccines are available to adults, adolescents, all people at any point in time... If you’re not vaccinated and you have the opportunity, get it." The Americas became the first region in the world to be free of measles in 2016 following a hugely successful vaccination campaign that health officials estimate prevented 6.2 million deaths between 2000 and 2023. analysis.brief_en: This article from HealthyChildren.org, published on November 24, 2026, offers general guidance on how to protect babies during a measles outbreak. It emphasizes the importance of vaccination, maintaining good hygiene, and avoiding exposure to infected individuals. The article does not provide specific data on cases, deaths, or exposures, nor does it detail any investigation or response activities. This has led to the virus becoming endemic, spreading within the population. The piece emphasizes the importance of having reliable diagnostic references for labs to ensure accurate and consistent testing results. However, it does not provide specific case counts, death tolls, or details on the measures taken by public health authorities to address the outbreak. The focus is on the challenges faced by diagnostic laboratories in maintaining test accuracy amid the rising number of measles cases.
news.content_zh: 文章讨论了 麻疹 在美国的死灰复燃,该国由于免疫率下降而失去了 麻疹 消除状态。这导致该病毒成为地方性流行病,在人群中传播。这篇文章强调了实验室拥有可靠的诊断参考以确保准确和一致的测试结果的重要性。然而,它没有提供具体的病例数、死亡人数或公共卫生当局为解决 暴发 问题而采取的措施的详细信息。重点是在 麻疹 病例数量不断增加的情况下,诊断实验室在保持测试准确性方面面临的挑战。
news.summary_zh: 文章讨论了 麻疹 在美国的死灰复燃,该国由于免疫率下降而失去了 麻疹 消除状态。这导致该病毒成为地方性流行病,在人群中传播。这篇文章强调了实验室拥有可靠的诊断参考以确保准确和一致的测试结果的重要性。然而,它没有提供具体的病例数、死亡人数或公共卫生当局为解决 暴发 问题而采取的措施的详细信息。重点是在 麻疹 病例数量不断增加的情况下,诊断实验室在保持测试准确性方面面临的挑战。

analysis_zh.location_and_population: 随着 麻疹 的回归,实验室需要可靠的诊断参考作者:Leka Papazisi,DVM,博士 | 2026 年 11 月 24 日 |阅读 5 分钟随着 麻疹 病例的增加以及越来越多的实验室建立自己的诊断测试,充分表征的参考材料可以使结果准确可靠。
analysis_zh.event: 由于免疫率下降导致病例增加,导致 麻疹病毒 流行,美国已失去 麻疹 消除状态。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 麻疹 病例正在攀升,但所提供的证据中没有报告具体的病例数、死亡人数或暴露人数。该风险被明确表述为在该国境内流行。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 文章强调,随着 麻疹 病例的增加,需要可靠的诊断参考,但它没有报告当局采取的具体调查、测试或遏制措施。

news.content: Skip to main content Download the AppGet your news faster with our mobile experience Install News Weather Features Eyewitness Mornings Chime In Watch Live Now 58° Sat 67° Sun 70° Sign In or Create Account Watch Kern County doctors urge vaccine checks ahead of Thanksgiving travel amid measles risk by Caroline Rowland Mon, November 23, 2026 at 11:45 AM Play/Pause Video Quality Speed0.25x0.5xnormal1.5x2x Audio Track Audio Quality Subtitlesopen Font sizedefault50%75%100%150%200%300%400% Font styledefaultitalicbold Font familydefaultmonospaced serifproportional serifmonospaced sans serifproportional sans serifcasualcursivesmall capital Font colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Font opacitydefault100%75%50%25% Character edgedefaultraiseddepresseduniformdrop shadowed Character edge colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Background colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Background opacitydefault100%75%50%25%0% Window colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Window opacitydefault100%75%50%25%0% BackReset 00:01 00:00 PlayMute Picture-in-PictureApple AirPlayGoogle CastVRSettingsFullscreen Replay logo 3VIEW ALL PHOTOS FILE - A nurse, prepares a combination measles, mumps and rubella vaccine for a patient at a pediatrics clinic in Easley, S.C., March 17, 2026. (AP Photo/Mary Conlon, File) 0Comment Share topics: Measles MMR Vaccination Kern County Thanksgiving Travel Airborne Virus CDC Pediatricians BAKERSFIELD, Calif. (KBAK/KBFX) — As families prepare to hit the road for Thanksgiving, local doctors in Kern County are urging people to double-check vaccination records after the county confirmed two travel-related measles cases in August. FILE - This undated image made available by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Feb. 4, 2015, shows an electron microscope image of a measles virus particle. (Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, via AP, File) Dr. William Franklin, an emergency room physician with Adventist Health, said unvaccinated travelers face higher risk of infection. “If you’ve not been immunized, your kids haven’t been immunized, they’re going to be at risk,” Franklin said. news.title_zh: 卡纳贝克县确诊 麻疹 (Rubeola) 病例 - moraminn.com
news.source_body_en: A confirmed measles (Rubeola) case has been identified in Kanabec County, Minnesota, according to a report by Kanabec County Community Health and the Minnesota Department of Health. The case was confirmed on November 27, 2026, and the health authorities are currently working to identify and contact individuals who may have been exposed. No additional cases, deaths, or exposures were reported, and the risk level was not explicitly stated. The response is ongoing, with contact tracing and investigation being conducted to manage the situation. The article highlights the collaboration between local health departments and state agencies to address the outbreak. No further details on the scale of the outbreak or specific prevention measures were provided in the evidence.
news.content_zh: 根据卡纳贝克县社区卫生部门和明尼苏达州卫生部的报告,明尼苏达州卡纳贝克县发现了一例 麻疹(Rubeola)确诊病例。该病例于 2026 年 11 月 27 日得到确认,卫生当局目前正在努力识别和联系可能接触过的个人。没有报告其他病例、死亡或暴露情况,也没有明确说明风险级别。应对工作正在进行中,正在进行接触者追踪和调查以控制局势。本文重点介绍了地方卫生部门和国家机构之间为解决 暴发 问题而进行的合作。证据中没有提供有关暴发规模或具体预防措施的进一步细节。

news.source_body_en: The article reports that the United States, Mexico, and Bolivia have lost their measles elimination status, as confirmed by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). This means that measles is no longer absent in these countries, indicating a resurgence of the disease. The article does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers, but it highlights the implications of this development. The loss of elimination status suggests that the countries may need to reassess their public health strategies to control the spread of measles. The article emphasizes the importance of addressing the issue to potentially regain elimination status in the future. The information is based on a news report published on 2026-11-26 by Medscape, which is a reputable medical news source.

supplementary_news.content_title: Measles resurges worldwide despite shrinking viral genetic diversity
supplementary_news.content: As measles cases rebound and rubella remains difficult to track, a 25-year global review examines how changing viral genetics and gaps in disease surveillance complicate efforts to eliminate both infections. Review: Global Update on Measles and Rubella Molecular Epidemiology: 2000–2025 . Image Credit: Yau Ming Low / Shutterstock In a recent review of global surveillance data published in the journal Vaccines , researchers investigated the molecular epidemiology of measles and rubella ( MR ) viruses worldwide between 2000 and 2025, examining sequence submissions and the distribution of viral genotypes. An international team of researchers from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), World Health Organization (WHO) headquarters and regional offices, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), and the Pasteur Institute of Tunis at University Tunis El Manar conducted the review, spanning institutions across nine countries. Measles virus ( MeV ) sequence submissions relative to reported cases have returned to pre-pandemic levels across all regions, but only two of the 24 historically recognized measles genotypes have been reported since 2021. The pandemic's impact on rubella surveillance remains difficult to determine, partly because few rubella virus ( RuV ) sequences are submitted to global surveillance databases. The review also outlines challenges facing the World Health Organization's ( WHO ) Global Measles and Rubella Laboratory Network ( GMRLN ) and stresses the need for continued member-state participation to strengthen molecular surveillance. Measles and rubella elimination remains a global public health priority. The WHO coordinates surveillance through GMRLN, which combines epidemiological reports and molecular data to track circulating strains and transmission. Member states contribute case reports and viral sequences to monitor genetic diversity, investigate outbreaks, and identify gaps in surveillance and vaccination. Global measles and rubella surveillance The review draws on global data from the Measles virus Nucleotide Surveillance ( MeaNS2 ) and Rubella virus Nucleotide Surveillance ( RubeNS2 ) databases through 2025. Most sequences are generated using reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction ( RT-PCR ) and Sanger sequencing. Only WHO GMRLN-accredited laboratories that pass annual laboratory proficiency tests can submit data. Member states must submit representative sequences covering 80% or more of transmission chains no later than eight weeks after sample receipt. MeV molecular surveillance relies mainly on the N-450 target, a 450-nucleotide segment located near the end of the nucleocapsid ( N ) gene. For RuV genotyping, laboratories examine a 739-nucleotide segment of the envelope glycoprotein 1 ( E1 ) gene, designated E-739 (739-bp window). The WHO compiles annual MR case figures using the Joint Reporting Form ( JRF ), developed jointly with UNICEF. MeV genotypes are classified according to sequence similarities in the hemagglutinin ( H ) and nucleoprotein (N) genes. Measles cases rebound after the pandemic A total of 411,913 measles cases were reported worldwide during 2025, returning to levels comparable to those before the pandemic. Reported cases are estimated to account for only around 5% of actual measles cases globally. Missed childhood vaccinations and resulting immunity gaps likely drove the resurgence. The extent to which pandemic-era declines reflected reduced transmission or disrupted surveillance remains unclear. Number of reported measles virus cases and sequence submissions to MeaNS2, stratified by WHO region. Reported case numbers were obtained from the WHO/UNICEF Joint Reporting Form (JRF), while sequence counts represent MeV sequences submitted by WHO GMRLN-accredited laboratories to MeaNS2. Transparency of grey bars indicates y-scale in that area of the plot and orders of magnitude between points. The European Region ( EUR ) recorded over 150,000 cases in 2024, its highest total since 1997, followed by a 75% decline in 2025. Cases rose from 2024 in the Region of the Americas ( AMR ), following previous regional measles elimination, while the African Region ( AFR ) and South-East Asia Region ( SEAR ) saw declines after their 2023 surges. Sequencing coverage was highest in the AMR, with a median annual ratio of submitted sequences to reported cases of 20% between 2000 and 2025, compared with 4% in the EUR and less than 1% in the other four WHO regions. Incomplete case reporting inflated AMR estimates, while representative outbreak sampling partly explains lower sequencing-to-case ratios in high-incidence regions. The EUR and Western Pacific Region ( WPR ) together contributed approximately 70% of sequences in MeaNS2. Annual distribution of MeV genotype B3 and D8 sequences submitted to MeaNS2, stratified by WHO region. Measles genetic diversity continues to decline The two remaining reported measles genotypes are B3 and D8. This reduction in genetic diversity is consistent with vaccination efforts limiting opportunities for viral transmission but makes distinguishing transmission chains through routine genotyping more difficult. D8 has been the most frequently reported genotype globally since 2018, except in 2021, and accounted for nearly all genetically characterized cases during the AMR resurgence in 2025. B3 was more common in the Eastern Mediterranean Region ( EMR ), while both genotypes were reported at comparable frequencies in the AFR and WPR. Europe also reported more B3 than D8 sequences in 2025 for the first time since 2021. Sequencing beyond the N-450 target has also increased since 2022, potentially improving transmission tracking. Among named strains, which represent frequently reported N-450 sequences, MVs/Gir Somnath.IND/42.16[D8] had the highest cumulative case count, with 6,595 recorded cases across 72 countries over a five-year period beginning in 2016. Rubella surveillance reveals major data gaps RuV molecular surveillance remains considerably more limited, with approximately one-tenth as many sequence submissions as measles. A shorter detection window, fewer detected cases, fewer accredited sequencing laboratories, lower viral RNA concentrations in clinical specimens, and the viral genome's high guanine-cytosine content may explain this gap. Rubella trends also varied by region. Reported cases in the AFR rose more than 20-fold, from 865 in 2000 to 19,669 in 2025, amid outbreaks in Nigeria, South Africa, and Uganda. The WPR peaked at 126,827 cases in 2008, before declining during 2020–2025. Some historical increases in reported cases may partly reflect improved surveillance sensitivity. Meanwhile, cases in the EUR and AMR fell approximately 1,000-fold since 2000. During the decade through 2025, approximately 247,000 rubella cases were reported globally, compared with more than 3.5 million measles cases. Incomplete reporting also means that the true rubella burden is likely higher. Fewer than one in 1,000 reported rubella cases were sequenced in previous years. Only 59 RuV sequences belonging to genotypes 1G and 2B were documented from 2022 onward, including just six in 2025. Genotype 2B has been the only genotype reported globally since 2024, while 1G, previously predominant in the AFR, was last reported in 2023. Genotype 1E predominated in the WPR during expanded surveillance between 2018 and 2020 but has not been reported since 2021. Limited sequencing coverage prevents definitive conclusions about whether other rubella genotypes have disappeared. Improving genomic surveillance and vaccination coverage “Sequence data alone cannot reliably reconstruct transmission patterns, particularly for measles.” Sustaining MR elimination will require investment in laboratory capacity, standardized sequencing protocols, quality assurance, surveillance, and vaccination. Whole-genome sequencing ( WGS ) and other extended sequencing approaches could improve the resolution of measles transmission tracking beyond the commonly used N-450 region. Their wider use is limited by costs, technical expertise, and inconsistent sequencing quality. Complete coding sequence ( CDS ) analysis could offer useful genetic detail while avoiding some technical challenges associated with non-coding regions, but its practical implementation would require high-throughput sequencing technology. Mutations identified through extended sequencing require interpretation alongside epidemiological data, case timing, and rates of genetic change in the virus, since longer genomic regions are naturally expected to contain more mutations. Named strains do not necessarily represent individual transmission chains. Differences in surveillance sensitivity, laboratory capacity, reporting completeness, and the proportion of laboratory-confirmed cases limit direct regional comparisons. Molecular surveillance must complement epidemiological investigations, with closer collaboration between laboratory scientists and epidemiologists needed to guide immunization efforts. No measles vaccine-escape strains have been reported. Maintaining high vaccination coverage and sensitive case detection remains central to MR elimination. Source: Journal reference: Weston, T., Cheng, C., Warrener, L. et al. (2026). Global Update on Measles and Rubella Molecular Epidemiology: 2000–2025. Vaccines , 14(11), 964. DOI : 10.3390/vaccines14110964, https://www.mdpi.com/2076-393X/14/11/964

supplementary_news.content_title: Measles outbreaks raise serious health concerns for expectant mothers and newborns
supplementary_news.content: As measles infections increasingly appear in U.S. adults-a new CDC report is raising concerns about a heightened risk of congenital measles and infections in pregnant women. For expectant mothers, evidence suggests that infections can increase the risk of non-labor related hospitalizations, pneumonia, and death. Congenital measles can occur when a pregnant woman becomes infected with measles during pregnancy and passes the virus to the fetus in the womb. Infants can face severe illness, encephalitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis-a rare, progressive, and often fatal neurological disorder. The new report, published in the New England Journal of Medicine Evidence, connects large measles outbreaks across the U.S. in 2025 and 2026 to 112 cases of measles in pregnant women and 13 cases of congenital measles in babies. In a November 25 episode of Public Health On Call, William Moss, MD, MPH, professor in Epidemiology, unpacks the new government analysis, including the measles threat to expectant mothers and newborns, and what it means in the context of ongoing outbreaks and the country's lapsed measles elimination status. Topics discussed: - The status of measles in the U.S., including current outbreaks in Pennsylvania and the nation's recent loss of elimination status - The new report from the CDC on congenital measles and why increases in adult measles infections are creating more openings for congenital measles - The possible health risks facing pregnant women who are infected with measles, and their newborns - How clinicians should approach measles vaccination and treatment for women of child-bearing age, pregnant women, and babies - The federal response to measles and congenital measles since 2025 Key quotes from the episode On the current status of measles and congenital measles in the U.S.: "Tragically we now have over 6,000 measles cases reported in the United States just this year." (01:54) "Earlier this month, on November 17, the Pan American Health Organization announced that the United States had lost its measles elimination status. Measles elimination is defined as no continuous transmission of the same measles virus strain for at least 12 months." (02:30) "A report from the Center for Disease Control and Prevention published in the New England Journal of Medicine Evidence ... report[ed] an astonishing 112 cases of measles in pregnant women and 13 cases of congenital measles." (03:10) "This is the largest case series that I'm aware of, of both measles in pregnancy and of congenital measles." (03:44) "According to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention, about 41% of measles cases in the United States have been in adults. If we look at Pennsylvania, for example, more than two-thirds of measles cases have been in adults 18 years or older." (04:02) "We're really seeing somewhat unusual demographic characteristics of the measles cases here in the United States, concentrated-or at least ... with high proportion-in adults." (04:18) On the health risks facing pregnant women who contract measles and their fetuses: "In the CDC report, almost a quarter of the women required hospitalization for non-labor related causes. Eleven of the 112, so about 10% of women, developed pneumonia. ... they're also at risk for serious birth outcomes: there can be stillbirths or miscarriages, premature births." (06:22) "During the last really big outbreak of measles here in the United States between 1989 and 1991 ... Pregnant women [with measles infections] were twice as likely to be admitted to the hospital, three times more likely to be diagnosed with pneumonia, and six times more likely to die of measles." (07:19) "We do know that infants ... with congenital measles can have some of the similar signs and symptoms of measles that we see in older children and adults: fever, rash." (8:10) "[Newborns are] also at risk for encephalitis, and there's even some suggestion ... that these infants may be at greater risk for a rare neurologic outcome called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis ... It's a severe, fatally progressive neurologic disease with a kind of defective measles virus in the brain." (08:27) On measles vaccination and treatment for pregnant women and infants: "Before pregnancy, make sure that you are vaccinated so that you are protected and can protect your infant." (15:37) "The measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is not indicated during pregnancy, and that's in part because of that immune-suppressed state of pregnant women and the fact that these are attenuated viral vaccines, so they need to replicate in order to induce an immune response. So, we can't vaccinate women during pregnancy." (09:54) "Instead of what we call active immunization-giving a vaccine and inducing that person's immune system to be trained to fight that pathogen-we give what's called passive immunization. And so, it's something called intravenous immunoglobulin." (10:30) "Immunoglobulin is also recommended at birth for newborns who have been exposed to measles virus in utero, if the mom has measles late in the third trimester or prior to birth, and that too can reduce the morbidity associated with congenital measles." (11:10) "During pregnancy, what women need to do is really ensure that the people around them, their family members, their friends who they're coming into contact with, are vaccinated against measles to really reduce their risk of exposure." (16:01) On the response to measles from federal health officials: "We've not seen the strong response from the federal government that is needed promoting measles vaccination, and, in fact, we've seen the opposite." (14:30) "We've seen messaging that undermines public confidence in vaccines in general and the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, specifically." (14:40) "I am sure that [the response from federal officials] has ... played a role in our loss of measles elimination status here in the United States and these continued large outbreaks. It's not the only explanation ... but the federal response has not helped and almost certainly set us back." (14:49)

supplementary_news.content: Nearly 6 in 10 Americans hold government leaders responsible for the loss of the United States' measles elimination status, according to a new Ipsos poll. But there are few signs that the public wants to dwell on it. Why it matters: Partisan divisions over vaccines and outbreaks are so entrenched that Democrats won't have a broad mandate beyond their base to investigate the government's response when they take control of Congress. - There's also a generational divide. People age 65 and over — who remember the introduction of the measles vaccine — are more likely to say the current situation bothers them a lot. What they found: Roughly 3 in 5 Americans (58%) think the loss of the measles elimination status could have been prevented if government leaders had done a better job encouraging people to get vaccinated and responding to outbreaks. - 38% said there wasn't much government leaders could have done, because people make their own health decisions. - There's a huge partisan split behind those numbers: 84% of Democrats say the return of measles could have been avoided if the government had done a better job, compared with 38% of Republicans. Just over a quarter of Americans (26%) say they're extremely or very concerned about an outbreak occurring in their community. - There's a nearly 30-percentage-point partisan gap on concern, with 42% of Democrats extremely or very concerned, compared with 13% of Republicans. Independents are in the middle (25%). The findings come as Americans are sharply divided over the prospect of the next Congress investigating the Trump administration. And if COVID-19 is any guide, the public tends to be eager to put public health calamities in the rearview. - A Reuters-Ipsos post-election poll found that just 10% of Republicans said they want the new Congress to focus a great deal or quite a bit on investigating the Trump administration, compared with 71% of Democrats. - "As frustrating as the loss of measles elimination status is for many Americans, there's little in the [new] survey to suggest it will lead people who were not already supportive of investigating the administration to prioritize congressional oversight on this issue," said Alec Tyson, senior vice president of Ipsos U.S. Public Affairs. That isn't discouraging some Democrats on Capitol Hill. Incoming Senate health committee Chair Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said last week that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s stewardship of the federal health apparatus during the measles outbreaks is "certainly one area that needs investigation." - House Energy and Commerce Democrats want to know whether the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suppressed the number of measles deaths reported to the public. - They've also criticized agency director Erica Schwartz for not providing meaningful answers about decision-making around the reporting and response. The CDC has said it's committed to stopping outbreaks and regaining the measles elimination status. - It has pointed to actions like providing about $100 million in extra funding to strengthen prevention and response to measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases. What we're watching: Support for childhood vaccinations appears stronger than in the immediate aftermath of the pandemic. - Gallup this week found that more than 7 in 10 say it is extremely or very important for parents to get their children vaccinated — with the share saying it is extremely important 7 percentage points higher than in 2024. Methodology: The Ipsos poll was conducted Nov. 20-23, 2026, by Ipsos' KnowledgePanel®. This poll is based on a nationally representative probability sample of 1,022 general population adults age 18 or older. - The margin of sampling error is +/-3.2 percentage points at the 95% confidence level, for results based on the entire sample of adults

supplementary_news.content: Health and Healthcare Systems US loses its status as measles-free, and other health stories Published Nov 24, 2026 A measles sign in New York.Image: REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton/File Photo After 26 years, the US can no longer claim to be free of measles following the continuing spread of the virus, while WHO and UNICEF are joining forces to tackle the global obesity issue. Read about these stories and more in this month’s round-up of top health news from around the world. 1. US declared no longer measles-free In a not-unexpected blow to the US, the country has lost its long-standing status of being free from the measles virus. Bolivia and Mexico have also lost their measles elimination status, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced on 17 November. The ruling “formalizes what was already plainly visible. The US has lost the ability to control measles," Dr Amesh Adalja, ​an infectious disease expert at the Johns Hopkins University Center for Health Security, told Reuters. Measles cases in the US have been on the increase in the past few years, with more than 2,200 cases recorded in 2025 and over 5,400 registered so far this year. This is compared to 59 cases in 2023 and 285 in 2024. Over 90% of the cases involve people who are unvaccinated, or their vaccination status is unknown, reports Science News. The affected countries will now need to prove that no one has caught measles within their borders for a full year in order to regain their measles-free status. To do so will require a huge turnaround in vaccination numbers, with 95% coverage required for herd immunity – as the chart above shows, coverage stood at 75% across the Americas in 2023. In response, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it had invested $100 million in vaccination programmes. Measles is on the rise once again. Here's how to fight it 01:42 2. WHO and UNICEF join forces to tackle global obesity issue More than 20 countries, led by Spain, have committed to a 5% reduction in national obesity rates by 2030, in a global call to action launched jointly by the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF. This amounts to five fewer obese people in every 100, says WHO and UNICEF, while pointing out that “halting the rise is the first milestone” in countries with the highest obesity rates. In 2024, one in seven people – or 1.1 billion – were living with obesity, which in an adult constitutes a BMI of at least 30. More than a third of adults across the Americas are obese and 170 million children globally are living with obesity. Indeed, “there are now more school-age children with obesity than children who are underweight,” pointed out WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus at the launch of the project. “If obesity were a virus, it would be called a pandemic, and the world would be racing to stop it.” Worldwide adult obesity has more than doubled since 1990.Image: Our World in Data With obesity thought to be behind 3.7 million deaths a year – by contributing to cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and cancers – tackling the issue is both a health and economic imperative. The joint obesity strategy calls on governments to prioritize obesity as a chronic disease, and align financial and policy support accordingly. “The costs of obesity are counted in years of life lost, in strained health systems, and in the children and adolescents whose futures are derailed by chronic disease and lasting complications,” said the joint report. Read more on this topic Health and Healthcare Systems Healthier for longer: Taking care of our ageing societies by addressing obesity 3. News in brief: Health stories from around the world Ebola outbreak still not under control: Six months after it was first declared, the Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo remains out of control, reports Reuters, with both cases of the disease and deaths as a result of it continuing to rise. Over 11,000 people have been infected and over 5,500 ⁠have died since the outbreak began in May, which is double the rate seen in the first six months of the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak. El Niño a threat to pregnant women: Midwives have warned that millions of women in countries rated high risk for El Niño are in danger of dying during childbirth because they won’t have access to hospitals or healthcare. About 15 million babies are due to be born during the peak El Niño period, representing two-thirds of births worldwide, reports the Guardian. Alzheimer’s breakthroughs: Two drug trials have shown some success in treating Alzheimer’s. One trial involved a medicine usually used to treat schizophrenia that helped alleviate the symptoms of psychosis experienced by some Alzheimer’s patients. While a drug which targets the toxic tau protein in the brain was shown to slow cognitive decline in early Alzheimer’s patients by 38% after two years, reports Reuters. Hormone-disrupting chemicals found pre-birth: Babies can be exposed to endocrine-disrupting chemicals before birth, which can have lasting effects on brain development and growth, according to a new report from the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and WHO. Exposure to these chemicals comes via everyday products and companies must work harder to “test early, disclose what is in their products, and get substitution right,” UNEP says. Eritrea eliminates trachoma: WHO has confirmed that Eritrea is the 11th African country and 34th globally to successfully eliminate trachoma – the leading infectious cause of blindness – as a public health problem. Globally, over 90 million people are still at risk of trachoma blindness. The news comes as the WHO presented its mid-term evaluation of its roadmap to eliminate neglected tropical diseases. Trachoma elimination stood at 65% in 2025 and the aim is for full elimination by 2030. Tuberculosis status update: WHO’s latest tuberculosis report finds that the global burden of TB is declining, with around 10.6 million people contracting the disease in 2025, a slight decrease on the previous year. That said, it’s still the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent and 2030 targets “remain distant”. 4. More on health from Forum Stories It’s estimated that around 80% of the world’s over-60s will be living in lower- and middle-income countries by 2030, with large numbers of these people in rural, underserved and impoverished areas. A coordinated effort is required to tackle this acute challenge, says Prakash Tyagi of GRAVIS. From pooling resources to transferring knowledge, this article gives a roadmap for government and societal response. Non-communicable diseases (NCD) cause three-quarters of deaths worldwide and 80% of those deaths are caused by just five conditions: heart disease, cancer, respiratory diseases, diabetes and kidney diseases. The following video explains the five key risk factors for developing an NCD – and the best prevention methods. These 5 health conditions cause the most deaths 01:58 The chronic underfunding of nurses is undermining a profession a conflicted world cannot do without, says the head of the International Council of Nurses. In this article, José Luis Cobos Serrano argues that the largest health workforce in the world needs to be better valued, empowered and backed by proper investment. “The strength of our health systems, our economies and our societies will depend largely on the decisions we make today regarding nursing,” he says. TBS Report 27 November, 2026, 04:05 pm Last modified: 27 November, 2026, 04:09 pm A mother carries her child suspected of having measles-like symptoms at a hospital in Bangladesh. File photo: UNB Seven more children died from measles and measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours until 8am today (27 November), taking the combined number of suspected and laboratory-confirmed measles-related deaths in Bangladesh to 1,378. Of the total deaths, 1,272 were suspected measles-related deaths, while 106 were confirmed through laboratory tests, according to the daily update of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). A total of 1,273 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, taking the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 2,62,808. Keep updated, follow The Business Standard's Google news channel Meanwhile, 78 new laboratory-confirmed cases were recorded, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 26,554. Since 15 March, a total of 2,35,482 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalised across the country. Of them, 2,26,440 have recovered, according to DGHS data. Set us as preferred To the editor: I took care of scores, if not hundreds, of children suffering from complications of measles, including pneumonia and encephalitis, over a period of three years as a pediatric house staff at a tertiary care center in India in the 1990s. Many of them died. I also saw subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, which is a less common but more lethal complication of measles. More recently, I was involved in an effort aimed at the education of U.S. physicians apropos neurological complications of vaccine-preventable diseases. The medical community in the U.S. is being prepared to handle the resurgence of diseases that many doctors here have never seen (“U.S. loses measles elimination status after first eradicating the disease 26 years ago,” Nov. 17). I am certain that they are going to be ready with the necessary knowledge. I am also certain that few are ready to handle the scars that come with taking care of children with devastating complications of easily preventable diseases. Jay Desai, Los Angeles This writer is a clinical professor at the University of Southern California and a neurologist at Children’s Hospital of Los Angeles.
